title: PCE Graphics in R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to create graphs for inclusion in papers or posters submitted for publication.

Plots
Please open the bpf dataset from the course website to complete this practicum. Please call the dataset bpf_data.
Before we begin, please note that R is an extremely flexible and powerful graphing tool. Nearly any graph you would like to make can be made using the plotting tools in R, but it may take a little patience to learn how to use the options. In this practicum, we will start by focusing on the options available in the plot command, but we will also introduce the ggplot2 library, which is a more flexible approach for plotting. We will start by creating a basic scatterplot that includes a single point per patient. On this graph, we also included basic axis labels. For the association between brain parenchymal fraction (BPF) and age, we show the basic command and resulting scatterplot here.

plot(x=bpf_data$age, y=bpf_data$bpf, xlab= "Age (years)", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction")








The first part of the command shows the x variable, and the second part of the command shows the y variable. In addition, the xlab and ylab options allow us to label the x-axis and y-axis, respectively.
Note that if you right click on the graph, you can save the graph or you can copy the graph and paste it into another program. R allows you to save the graph in several formats that are commonly used by journals, including .eps and .emf. You can also create a .pdf or .ps file with the graph.
R allows flexibility in terms changing parts of a graph. In particular, if you would like to use filled in red plus signs for each of the points, you can add options shown here. The options pch changes the marker (blue arrow) and col changes the color (red arrow). Many additional options are available, and you can learn more about these by looking at the help menu for par and points using ?par and ?points.

plot(x=bpf_data$age, y=bpf_data$bpf, xlab= "Age (years)", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction", pch=3, col="red")








###Graphs for subsets of data
This dataset consisted of both men and women, and we might be interested in plotting the data for just the men. To do this in R, we can subset the dataset as we have seen previously using the following command:

plot(x=bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==1], y=bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==1], xlab= "Age (years)", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction", main="Disease activity")








Note that we were able to add a title “Disease activity” to the graph by adding the main option to the command as well.


Multiple groups on the same graph
As an alternative, you might want to create a graph with different markers for each group. To do this in R, we can use a similar command that creates a scatterplot for each group. To ensure that the plot is the correct size, it is often best to create a blank plot with the entire dataset using the same command as above including type=”n” to indicate that we would like a blank plot.
Once we have produced the blank plot, we can add the points for the two groups separately using the points command. Within each points command, we will use the pch and col options. For the disease activity group, we will use black open circles. For the no disease activity group, we will use red solid circles.
If you were interested in adding a legend to the graph, you can use the legend command. The first part of the command shows the desired location of the legend, which is the bottom left of the graph in this case. Then, we specify what we like the legend to say for each of the point types. Specifically, we use the label “Activity” for the black open circles, and we use the label “No activity” for the red closed circles.

plot(x=bpf_data$age, y=bpf_data$bpf, xlab= "Age (years)", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction", type="n")

points(x=bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==1], y=bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==1])
points(x=bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==0], y=bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==0], col="red", pch=19)

legend("bottomleft", c("Activity", "No activity"), pch=c(1,19), col=c("black","red"))










Adding a best fit line
Another common thing to add to a scatterplot is a best fit line. A best fit line is usually calculated using linear regression, and R allows you to easily add a best fit line from linear regression. First, we must calculate the best fit line using linear regression with the lm and predict commands.

lm.res<-lm(bpf~age, data=bpf_data)
bpf_data$predbpf<-predict(lm.res)

If you look at the bpf_data dataset, you can see that the predicted BPF based on the linear model has been added for each patient. We can add the best fit line to the original graph by first plotting the original data using the command from above. To add the best fit line, we use the lines command. The x-variable is still age, but the y-variable for the best fit line is the predicted value, predbpf.

plot(x=bpf_data$age, y=bpf_data$bpf, xlab= "Age (years)", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction")

lines(x=bpf_data$age, y=bpf_data$predbpf)










Continuous outcome and categorical predictor
Another common graph is to plot the values of a continuous outcome with a categorical predictor. In our present dataset, we may want to plot BPF and activity on a scatterplot to look at the individual data points. In this case, activity is a categorical variable and BPF is a continuous variable. The following plot command has the same format as above, but since activity is a factor variable, R will produce group specific box plots.

plot(x=factor(bpf_data$activity), y=bpf_data$bpf, xlab= "Disease activity", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction")








To create a plot with the individual points, we can use the numeric variable “activity”. When we use the plot command, we can show the individual points, but we would like to adjust the x-axis to show which group is the disease activity group and the no disease activity group. First, we must remove the default x-axis using the xaxt part of the command. Then, we can add our own x-axis using the axis command. For this command, we must specify the axis we want to draw, and the value “1” means the bottom axis (blue arrow). The at command says where we would like to place the labels. The labels command states the labels that will be placed at each of the at values. Since “activity” takes on values 0 and 1, we use these in the at command (red arrow) and we provide the appropriate labels in the labels command (green arrow).

plot(x=bpf_data$activity, y=bpf_data$bpf, xlab= "Disease activity", ylab="Brain parenchymal fraction",xaxt="n")
axis(1,at=c(0,1),labels=c("No activity","Activity"))








As you can see from these brief examples, there are many options available in plotting graphs in R so please explore to learn more.

title: PCE Graphics in R
text:
Bonus material
In this section, we will learn about making many of the plots in the previous section using the ggplot2 library. The ggplot2 library is part of the tidyverse, which is a set of R libraries that can be quite powerful. We will learn more about the using the tidyverse for data management as well. Let’s start by installing the tidyverse, which includes ggplot2. You need to use install.packages(“tidyverse”) once, and then use the library command in each R session.

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.1.4     ✔ readr     2.1.6
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.2     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.1     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors


Although I will introduce you to ggplot, this website provides great additional references and a cheat sheet for using ggplot. Please see this website for more information after you complete this practicum.
ggplot2
Also, you can access an excellent “Cheat sheet” for ggplot here:
ggplots2 cheatsheet
Let’s start by making a scatterplot using ggplot. We can to create a blank plot for a specific dataset using the ggplot command. The way to put a plot in the blank plot is to add layers to the graph. To add a scatterplot, we use the geom_point command, which adds points to the plot:

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age,y=bpf))








We can add labels for the x-axis and y-axis using the following labs command added to the previous command:

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age,y=bpf))+
labs(x= "Age (years)", y="Brain parenchymal fraction")








We can make the plot showing the two groups in different colors using this ggplot command, which adds the color=factor(activity) option to the geom_points command. This makes the points separately for each value of activity and provides a legend showing how to identify the colors. Other options for this can be used to change the fill, size, and shape using similar syntax.

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf, color=factor(activity)))+
labs(x= "Age (years)", y="Brain parenchymal fraction")








To plot only those with disease activity, we can use this ggplot command:

ggplot(data=bpf_data[bpf_data$activity== 1,]) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf))+
labs(x= "Age (years)", y="Brain parenchymal fraction")








In the plot commands above, we could add the best fit line to the plot by calculating the predicted value and adding the line. In ggplot, we can add a second plot layer for the best fit line using the geom_smooth command:

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf))+
geom_smooth(method=lm, se=F, mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf))+
labs(x= "Age (years)", y="Brain parenchymal fraction")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









The se=F option removes the confidence standard error for the best fit line.
We can also add the best fit line using the predicted values from above by adding a different layer:

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf))+
geom_line(mapping=aes(x=age, y=predbpf))+
labs(x= "Age (years)", y="Brain parenchymal fraction")








The geom_smooth command without the method=lm option will provide a loess smoothed fit, which does not assume a linear relationship between the predictor and the outcome.

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf))+
geom_smooth(mapping=aes(x=age, y=bpf))+
labs(x= "Age (years)", y="Brain parenchymal fraction")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









Finally, we can make the plot showing the BPF in the disease activity group and no disease activity group using these commands:

ggplot(data=bpf_data) +
geom_point(mapping=aes(y=bpf, x=factor(activity)))








There are many other options that ggplot allows so please try different options out to see learn more about this command.

title: PCE Practicum Ttest for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to create new variables, complete a two-sample t-test, and complete a Wilcoxon rank sum test in R.

One sample analysis of a continuous outcome
Please load the MSQOL dataset into R. Please note that we have a large sample size so we will use the t-test for the analysis without assessing normality, but you can use the approaches from the previous section to assess normality if you were interested.
Based on your prior knowledge, you know that the general population has a mean score on the mental composite summary (MCS) for the SF-36 of 50 units. We would like to estimate the mean MCS score (variable name in the dataset: mcs). Note that the MCS does not have units, so we will just use the term “units” to remind ourselves to report units in our analysis.
The steps for an analysis are:

State estimand of interest
State type of data
Determine appropriate statistical method
State estimate
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package)
Interpret confidence interval and p-value with a focus on precision

Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our analysis:

State estimand of interest: Mean MCS score
State type of data: Continuous outcome, single sample
Determine appropriate statistical test: one sample t-test

R will allow us to calculate our summary statistics, confidence interval and p-value using a single command, t.test. For the one sample t-test, we need to specify the variable of interest first as well as the value for the null hypothesis, 50:
t.test(msqol$mcs,mu=50)
Here is the output of the command:

t.test(msqol$mcs,mu=50)


    One Sample t-test

data:  msqol$mcs
t = -1.228, df = 250, p-value = 0.2206
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 50
95 percent confidence interval:
 48.14726 50.42966
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 49.28846 


The output presented here provides the sample mean (49.3 units). The output also presents the 95% confidence interval for the mean (48.1, 50.4). In addition to this information, R provides the two-sided alternative hypothesis, which corresponds to the p-value (p=0.221).
With this information, we can complete our hypothesis test.

State estimate: \(\bar{x}\) = 49.3 units
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package) 95% CI: 48.1, 50.4; p=0.221
Interpret confidence interval and p-value with a focus on precision: The estimated mean MCS score was 49.3 units, and the range of plausible values is from 48.1 to 50.4 units. The mean in the normal population (50) is included in the confidence interval

In addition to the fitting the one-sample t-test, we might want to assess if the assumptions of the one-sample t-test are met. For the one-sample t-test, this means assessing whether the data come from a normal distribution. Remember with the sample size of 251 observations, the one-sample t-test is appropriate even if the data do not come from a normal distribution because the one-sample t-test is robust to departures from normality with a moderate to large sample size.
In order to assess the normality assumption, we will use summary statistics, graphics, and formal statistical tests. To calculate the summary statistics, we can use the summary, sd, skewness, and kurtosis commands. Remember that we need to load the e1071 library for the skewness and kurtosis commands

library(e1071)
summary(msqol$mcs)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  18.38   44.26   51.47   49.29   56.30   65.78       1 

sd(msqol$mcs,na.rm=T)

[1] 9.17998

skewness(msqol$mcs,na.rm=T)

[1] -0.9822499

kurtosis(msqol$mcs,na.rm=T)

[1] 0.5286531


The results of the commands are shown. The reported summary statistics include the mean (49.3), standard deviation (9.18), skewness (-0.98), and kurtosis (0.53). The negative value for the skewness indicates that the data will be skewed to the left, which we will see in the histogram below. The minimum, maximum, and quartiles are also shown in the summary output.
In addition to the summary statistics, we can create a histogram using the hist command and a QQ-plot using the qqnorm command.

hist(msqol$mcs)







qqnorm(msqol$mcs)
qqline(msqol$mcs)








Finally, shapiro.test provides the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality. From the Shapiro-Wilk test, we can see that the p-value is less than 0.0001, meaning that there is evidence that the data do not come from a normal distribution.

shapiro.test(msqol$mcs)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  msqol$mcs
W = 0.92553, p-value = 6.568e-10


Despite the evidence of a departure from a normal distribution, we will use the one-sample t-test results because the sample size is large enough.


Two sample t-test
Another question of interest based on this initial dataset is whether the mental quality of life as measured by MCS is different in male vs. female RRMS patients. We assume that the male and female RRMS patients in our study represent a random sample of the male and female RRMS patients.
As always, we can complete the first three steps of the analysis prior to looking closely at the data.

State estimand of interest: \(μ_{females}-μ_{males}\)
State the type of data: Continuous outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical method: Two sample t-test

As before, R will allow us to calculate our summary statistics and p-value using a single command, t.test. For the two sample t-test, we need to specify the outcome variable first and the group variable second. We separate the outcome and group variable with ~. Note that the default in R is to fit an unequal variance t-test. Since we would like to run this type of t-test, no additional options are required.

t.test(msqol$mcs~msqol$male)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  msqol$mcs by msqol$male
t = 1.5371, df = 93.824, p-value = 0.1276
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 0 and group 1 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.6150422  4.8314837
sample estimates:
mean in group 0 mean in group 1 
       49.77562        47.66740 


The output presented here provides the means in the two groups, from which you can calculate the difference (49.8-47.7 = 2.1 units). The output also presents the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the mean (-0.6, 4.8). In addition to this information, R provides the two-sided alternative hypothesis, which corresponds to the p-value (p=0.128, orange arrow).
With this information, we can complete our analysis.

State estimate: \(\bar{x}_{females}-\bar{x}_{males}\)=2.1 units
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 95% CI: -0.6, 4.8; p=0.128
The estimated difference in mean MCS score comparing females to males was 2.1 units, and the range of plausible values is from -0.6 to 4.8 units. The confidence interval includes values showing that males have a slightly higher MCS score or females have higher MCS scores.

If we had completed the analysis assuming equal variances, we would have arrived at the same conclusion. Please try this on your own.
t.test(msqol$mcs~msqol$male,var.equal=T)
As you learned in class, the two-sample t-test requires a normality assumption. We can assess the normality assumption using both graphical approaches and statistical tests. First, we make histograms and QQ-plots separately in the two groups.

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(msqol$mcs[msqol$male==0])
hist(msqol$mcs[msqol$male==1])







par(mfrow=c(1,2))
qqnorm(msqol$mcs[msqol$male==0])
qqline(msqol$mcs[msqol$male==0])
qqnorm(msqol$mcs[msqol$male==1])
qqline(msqol$mcs[msqol$male==1])








Each of these graphs show that the data do not follow a normal distribution. From the histogram, we can see the skewness in the data by observing the right tail. From the QQ-plot, we can see that the points do not sit on the line.
In terms of formal statistical tests, we can use the Shapiro-Wilks test in each group separately using the by command. For this, we type the by command. Next, we choose the variable that we want to analyze (mcs). Then, we specify the variable that defines the groups (male). Finally, we write the command we want to use (shapiro.test).
The results of the command are shown here:

by(msqol$mcs, msqol$male, shapiro.test)

msqol$male: 0

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  dd[x, ]
W = 0.91323, p-value = 3.123e-09

------------------------------------------------------------ 
msqol$male: 1

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  dd[x, ]
W = 0.94847, p-value = 0.01549


We can see that the Shapiro-Wilk tests in each group show that there is evidence against the data coming from a normal distribution (male=0 first and male=1 second) because both the p-values are small.
As in the one sample case, we can use the two-sample t-test results in this case because we have a sufficient sample size for the results to be valid even with data that do not come from a normal distribution. Alternative approach in the presence of a departure from normality are to switch to a nonparametric test to compare the groups or to transform the data and compare the transformed variable using a two-sample t-test. When we switch to a nonparametric test, the most common approach is the Wilcoxon rank sum test, which we can fit in R using the wilcox.test command. This command is very similar to the t.test command:

wilcox.test(msqol$mcs~msqol$male)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  msqol$mcs by msqol$male
W = 6448, p-value = 0.0794
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


The p-value for the test of the null hypothesis of the same distribution in the two groups is 0.0794 (blue arrow).
Finally, let’s show how to use a log transformation. Note that the data in this case is left skewed so a log transformation would not be an appropriate transformation. A different variable in the dataset that is right skewed and therefore might benefit from a log transformation is fatigue. We can see the distribution of fatigue using histogram.

hist(msqol$fatig)








To generate the log transformed version of fatigue, we create a new variable in the msqol data frame. In this command, we provide the name of the new variable (logfatig) and the formula for the value of the new variable on the right side of the <- symbol. Note that we need to add 1 to the fatigue score to account for the 0’s in the dataset.

msqol$logfatig<-log(msqol$fatig+1)

Now, we can look at the distribution of the new variable using histogram. In this case, the log transformation has not led to a normal distribution so one of the previous analyses should be used.

hist(msqol$logfatig)

title: PCE Practicum Summary Statistics for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to calculate summary statistics and how to make simple graphics in R.

Summary statistics
In lecture, we investigated summary statistics and basic graphics. In this practicum, we will learn how to calculate summary statistics and create graphics in R.
Please read the digitalis_dataset_23.csv dataset into R by following the steps from the previous document and call the dataset dig for the remaining code below. R is case sensitive. This means that you should check if the variable names are uppercase or lowercase. In the remainder of this practicum, we will use lowercase for the variable names, but you can adjust as needed.
On Canvas, we also provide a PDF describing the Digitalis trial, which was a multicenter trial with more than 300 centers in the US and Canada. This trial aimed to estimate the efficacy and safety of Digoxin in treating patients with congestive heart failure. A teaching version of the dataset has been made available by the NHBLI, and information related to the dataset is also provided on Canvas. Please note that this dataset is only a subset of the full dataset available from NHBLI.
An important first step in many studies is to calculate summary statistics related to baseline characteristics in the sample. To calculate the summary statistics for a continuous variable, the R command summary can be used. Let’s investigate baseline age using the summary. For this command, we write the command first (summary). Then, inside the parentheses we list the dataset name before the dollar sign (dig) and the variable name within the dataset after the dollar sign (age). The following output is produced:

summary(dig$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.62   71.00   90.00 


In this output, R provides the minimum (21), median (65), mean (63.6), and maximum (90).
We can also calculate additional summary statistics using separate commands. Note that for these commands, we would need to add the na.rm=T option if there were missing observations in the dataset. Here are the commands and output for calculating the mean, standard deviation, and variance.

mean(dig$age)

[1] 63.61786

sd(dig$age)

[1] 10.85402

var(dig$age)

[1] 117.8098


If we would like to calculate the median, minimum and maximum, we can use the following commands:

median(dig$age)

[1] 65

min(dig$age)

[1] 21

max(dig$age)

[1] 90


If we would like to calculate other percentiles, we can use the quantile command with the probs option to indicate the percentile we are interested in. As an example, this command will calculate the 25th and 75th percentiles.

quantile(dig$age, probs=c(0.25, 0.75))

25% 75% 
 57  71 


To calculate the skewness and kurtosis, we need to install a separate library. In R, there are libraries that we can install with additional commands.

library(e1071)
skewness(dig$age)

[1] -0.5246339

kurtosis(dig$age)

[1] 0.2909112




Graphics
R has the ability to create many graphics. Although there are advanced R packages to create plots, we will focus on basic R commands at this early stage. When we make plots in RStudio, the resulting plots are shown in the lower right-hand window. We can copy and paste the plots or save the plots using the Export button above the plot.
For the histogram of age, we use the following command.

hist(dig$age, xlab="Age", main="Histogram of Age")








For this command, age is the variable name for the variable of interest. The other two options tell R the title of the x-axis and the title of the graph.
For the box plot of age, we use the following command:

boxplot(dig$age, ylab="Age", main="Box plot of Age")










Proportion
In the dataset, the variable “sex” is a dichotomous variable, so the summary statistic of interest is the proportion of males and females. As described above, sex=1 for male and sex=2 for the female. To calculate the frequency and proportion of males and females in the dataset, we can use the table and prop.table commands.

table(dig$sex)


   1    2 
4216 1227 


This command provides the number of males (4216) and females (1227).

prop.table(table(dig$sex))


        1         2 
0.7745728 0.2254272 


This command provides the percent of males (0.7745728) and females (0.2254272).


Group specific summary statistics
In addition to the summary statistics in the entire sample, we would often like to calculate the summary statistics in each sex separately. In R, there are a number of ways to calculate the group specific summary statistics. One approach to calculate the age in each group is to subset the data and calculate the summary statistics in each subset. To subset the data, we can choose the rows from the dataset with sex=1. Then, we can calculate the summary statistics of the age in this subset.
For this command, note that we have the same information as the original summary command from above. In particular, we are applying the summary command (summary) to the variable age from the dataset dig. The main change is that we have added [dig$sex==1,] . When we use the [], we are trying to look at a subset of the data. When we have a data frame, there are both rows and columns. The rows that we would like to focus on are identified before the comma, and the columns after the comma. By writing dig$sex==1 before the comma, we indicate that we would like the rows in which sex is equal to 1. Since we have nothing after the comma, we indicate that we would like all the columns. The result is that dig[dig$sex==1,] finds the rows in the dig dataset in which sex is equal to 1, and then the rest of the command find the summary statistics for the variable age. We can use the same concept for sex equal to 2.

summary(dig[dig$sex==1,]$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  22.00   57.00   65.00   63.54   71.00   90.00 

summary(dig[dig$sex==2,]$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.89   71.00   90.00 


An alternative approach is to use the by command. In this command, we state the variable we are interested in (dig$age), the variable that identifies the groups (dig$sex), and the function we would like to apply to the variable (summary).

by(dig$age, dig$sex, summary)

dig$sex: 1
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  22.00   57.00   65.00   63.54   71.00   90.00 
------------------------------------------------------------ 
dig$sex: 2
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.89   71.00   90.00

title: PCE Practicum Proportions for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to do analysis of proportions in R.

Confidence intervals for a single proportion
For this analysis, we will use the MSQOL dataset. Please read this dataset into R.
We would like to estimate the proportion of RRMS patients with fatigue scores of at least 40. To calculate a confidence interval for this proportion, we will dichotomize fatigue using 40 as the cut-off. First, we will create a new variable called fatiglevel. We will assign fatiglevel=0 if fatigue score is less than 40 and fatiglevel=1 if fatigue score is greater than or equal 40. In R, a shorthand approach for creating this variable is to use the ifelse command. First, we must provide a name of the new variable that we are creating, which is fatiglevel (msqol$fatiglevel). Then, we will use the ifelse command, which has three parts. The first part is the condition that we are testing (msqol$fatig>=40). If the condition is true, fatiglevel will be assigned the value in the second part, which is 1 in this case. If the condition is false, fatiglevel will be assigned the value in the third part, which is 0. Now, we can calculate the number and proportion of subject with and without high fatigue.

msqol$fatiglevel<-ifelse(msqol$fatig>=40,1,0)
table(msqol$fatiglevel)


  0   1 
208  44 

prop.table(table(msqol$fatiglevel))


        0         1 
0.8253968 0.1746032 


The estimated proportion of patients with fatigue score greater than or equal to 40 is \(\hat{p}=\) 0.175.
To calculate the exact binomial confidence interval for the proportion, we can use the binom.test command. For this command, we can specify the number of successes in the first part of the command and the number of observations in the second part. Note that table(msqol$fatiglevel)[2] is one approach to calculate the number of patients with fatigue score greater than or equal to 40, and sum(table(msqol$fatiglevel)) is one approach to calculate the total number of observations with a fatigue score.

binom.test(x=table(msqol$fatiglevel)[2],n=sum(table(msqol$fatiglevel)))


    Exact binomial test

data:  table(msqol$fatiglevel)[2] and sum(table(msqol$fatiglevel))
number of successes = 44, number of trials = 252, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1298262 0.2272180
sample estimates:
probability of success 
             0.1746032 


The estimated proportion is the same as above (\(\hat{p}=\) 0.175) and the 95% confidence interval is shown as well (0.13, 0.227). Note that a hypothesis test for the null hypothesis that the true probability of success is equal to 0.5 is also provided. Often, this hypothesis test is not of interest so be careful interpreting this p-value. You can change the null hypothesis to be 0.2, which was the hypothesis from class, by adding \(p=0.2\) to the end of the command. Please see ?binom.test for more information.
As described in lecture, other potential confidence intervals are sometimes used as well and these are easily implemented in R. For example, the Wilson confidence interval, which is recommended by many authors, can be calculated using the prop.test command. Note that this command is very similar to the binom.test command, but we must include the correct=F option to get the Wilson interval.

prop.test(x=table(msqol$fatiglevel)[2],n=sum(table(msqol$fatiglevel)), correct=F)


    1-sample proportions test without continuity correction

data:  table(msqol$fatiglevel)[2] out of sum(table(msqol$fatiglevel)), null probability 0.5
X-squared = 106.73, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1327152 0.2262628
sample estimates:
        p 
0.1746032 


Note that the estimated proportion is the same as above, but the confidence interval has changed slightly. Note that a hypothesis test for the null hypothesis that the true probability of success is equal to 0.5 is also provided as in the binom.test command, but we can change this by adding another part to the command.


Two sample test of proportions
In lecture, we investigated the effect of a single nucleotide polymorphism on the probability of disease progression in patients with multiple sclerosis. The dataset for this analysis is the 2x2table.csv dataset. In this dataset, we have the variable snp that equals 1 for patients with the SNP and 0 for patients without the SNP, and we have the variable prog that equals 1 for patients who progressed and 0 for patients who failed to progress.
Please load the 2x2table.csv dataset into R and call the dataset, snp_data.
Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State estimand of interest: \(p_{SNP-}-p_{SNP+}\)
State the type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical method: Two sample test of proportions

In this case, we would like to estimate the difference in the probability of progression patients without the SNP and those with the SNP. First, let’s look at a cross tabulation of the data. Create a table using snp as the row variable and prog as the column variable:

table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog)

   
      0   1
  0 103  13
  1  62  12


Of those patients without the SNP (top row), 13 progressed, and 103 failed to progress. Of those patients with the SNP (bottom row), 12 progressed, and 62 failed to progress.
Now let’s look at a table of the row proportions. When we add the option 1 to the prop.table, we get the row proportions. If we use the option 2, we get column proportions. If we do not add an option to prop.table, we get total sample proportions.

prop.table(table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog),1)

   
            0         1
  0 0.8879310 0.1120690
  1 0.8378378 0.1621622


Of those patients without the SNP, 0.112 progressed, and 0.888 failed to progress. Of those patients with the SNP, 0.162 progressed, and 0.838 failed to progress.
There are a number of ways to complete this analysis in R. The first is to complete a test of proportions using the prop.test command. This test provides you with the summary statistics as well as the p-value for the hypothesis test. The correct=FALSE option specifies that we are not using the continuity correction in our test. The default uses the continuity correction.

prop.test(table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog),correct=FALSE)


    2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity correction

data:  table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog)
X-squared = 0.99215, df = 1, p-value = 0.3192
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.0516337  0.1518201
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.8879310 0.8378378 


The output presented here provides the sample proportions in each group. R reports the proportion that failed to progress (\(prog=0\)) rather than the proportion that progressed (\(prog=1\)). The estimated difference in the proportion who failed to progress is \(\hat{q}_{SNP-}-\hat{q}_{SNP+}=\) 0.888 \(-\) 0.838= 0.05. Note that we use the notation \(\hat{q}\) for the proportion who failed to progress as opposed to \(\hat{p}\) which represented the proportion who progressed. The output also presents the Wald 95% confidence interval for the difference of the proportions (\(\hat{q}_{SNP-}-\hat{q}_{SNP+}\): -0.052, 0.152). Finally, R provides the two-sided hypothesis test p-value (\(p=\) 0.319).
If we wanted R to report the proportion who progressed in the two groups we could use this command.

prop.test(table(snp_data$snp,(1-snp_data$prog)),correct=F)  


    2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity correction

data:  table(snp_data$snp, (1 - snp_data$prog))
X-squared = 0.99215, df = 1, p-value = 0.3192
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.1518201  0.0516337
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.1120690 0.1621622 


Note that the p-value and the conclusion is the same as above, but the confidence interval has the opposite sign. The sign of the confidence limits has changed because the estimated difference between the proportions is now the proportion that progressed in SNP- minus proportion that progressed in SNP+ \(\hat{p}_{SNP-}-\hat{p}_{SNP+}=\) 0.05.
With this information, we can complete our analysis.

State estimate: \(\hat{p}_{SNP-}-\hat{p}_{SNP+}=\) 0.05
Calculate 95% confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 95% CI: -0.052, 0.152; \(p=\) 0.319
Write conclusion: Based on our sample, the range of plausible values for the difference in the proportions is -0.052 to 0.152. No difference between the groups is one of the plausible values.



Chi-squared test
The more common way to test the same hypothesis is to use a chi-square test, and the chisq.test command will run the chi-square test. Again, the default uses the continuity correction, while the correct=FALSE option will turn it off:

chisq.test(table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog),correct=FALSE)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog)
X-squared = 0.99215, df = 1, p-value = 0.3192


The results from above provide the p-value for the test of an association between the two measures (\(p=\) 0.319). There is no estimate of the association from this command, but we will show how to get an estimate of the association from another command.


Fisher’s exact test
We can test the same hypothesis with Fisher’s exact test. The first three steps of the hypothesis test are the same as above, but we use the fisher.test command:

fisher.test(table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog))


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  table(snp_data$snp, snp_data$prog)
p-value = 0.3803
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.596721 3.896397
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
  1.529888 


The results from above provide the p-value for the test of an association between the two measures (\(p=\) 0.38).


Estimates of association
In order to calculate other estimates of the association when we have a dichotomous predictor and a dichotomous outcome, we can use the extensive set of commands in the epitools library. Within this library, there are separate commands for the calculation of the risk ratio and odds ratio. Note that we used the prop.test command to calculate the risk difference and the associated 95% confidence interval. To calculate risk ratio, we install the library and use riskratio command. For this command, we list the predictor (snp) as “x” and the outcome (prog) as “y”, and we get the following results:

library(epitools)
riskratio(x=snp_data$snp,y=snp_data$prog)

$data
         Outcome
Predictor   0  1 Total
    0     103 13   116
    1      62 12    74
    Total 165 25   190

$measure
         risk ratio with 95% C.I.
Predictor estimate     lower    upper
        0 1.000000        NA       NA
        1 1.446985 0.6984203 2.997861

$p.value
         two-sided
Predictor midp.exact fisher.exact chi.square
        0         NA           NA         NA
        1  0.3303927    0.3802594  0.3192177

$correction
[1] FALSE

attr(,"method")
[1] "Unconditional MLE & normal approximation (Wald) CI"


From this set of results, we get both the chi-squared test p-value (0.319) and Fisher’s exact test p-value (0.38). Further, we get the estimated risk ratio (1.45) and the associated 95% confidence interval (0.7, 3). Using these results, we can perform our analysis:

State estimand of interest: \(\frac{p_{SNP+}}{p_{SNP-}}\); \(H_0: \frac{p_{SNP+}}{p_{SNP-}}=1\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical test: Chi-squared test with risk ratio estimate
State estimate: \(\hat{RR}=\frac{\hat{p}_{SNP+}}{\hat{p}_{SNP-}}\) = 1.45
Calculate 95% confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 95% CI: 0.7, 3; \(p=\) 0.319
Write conclusion: Based on our sample, the range of plausible values for the risk ratio is 0.7 to 3. No difference between the groups is one of the plausible values.

To calculate odds ratio, we can use the oddsratio command. For this command, we list the predictor as “x” and the outcome as “y”, and we get the following results:

oddsratio(x=snp_data$snp,y=snp_data$prog)

$data
         Outcome
Predictor   0  1 Total
    0     103 13   116
    1      62 12    74
    Total 165 25   190

$measure
         odds ratio with 95% C.I.
Predictor estimate    lower    upper
        0 1.000000       NA       NA
        1 1.531089 0.644222 3.615143

$p.value
         two-sided
Predictor midp.exact fisher.exact chi.square
        0         NA           NA         NA
        1  0.3303927    0.3802594  0.3192177

$correction
[1] FALSE

attr(,"method")
[1] "median-unbiased estimate & mid-p exact CI"


From this set of results, we get both the chi-squared test p-value (0.319) and Fisher’s exact test p-value (0.38). Further, we get the estimated odds ratio (1.53) and the associated 95% confidence interval (0.64, 3.62). Using these results, we can perform our analysis:

State estimand of interest: \(\frac{Odds_{SNP+}}{Odds_{SNP-}}\); \(H_0: OR = \frac{Odds_{SNP+}}{Odds_{SNP-}} =1\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical test: Chi-squared test with odds ratio estimate
State estimate: \(\hat{OR} = \frac{\hat{Odds}_{SNP+}}{\hat{Odds}_{SNP-}}=\) 1.53
Calculate 95% confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 95% CI: 0.64, 3.62; \(p=\) 0.319
Write conclusion: Based on our sample, the range of plausible values for the odds ratio is 0.64 to 3.62. No difference between the groups is one of the plausible values.

title: PCE Practicum Survival for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: In this practicum, we will learn how to handle dates, declare data as survival data, create Kaplan-Meier curves and perform a log-rank test in R

Introduction
Time to event data is extremely common in medical research. Time to event data is more complex than traditional continuous outcomes because two or three pieces of information are involved. In the simple case of a time to event when every starts at the same point (i.e. the beginning of a clinical trial), the two pieces of information are the time to event and an indicator of whether the event is a failure time or a censoring time. Common notation for this is (\(X_i\), \(\delta_i\)) where \(X_i\) is the time to event (minimum of either the failure time or censoring time) and \(\delta_i\) is the failure indicator.


Declaring survival time data
Please read in the relapse dataset.
In order to complete a survival analysis in R, we must declare the data to be survival data. A common format for survival data is to have two variables define the outcome: (1) survival/ censoring time (\(X_i\)) and (2) failure indicator (\(\delta_i\)). In the relapse dataset, we have a variable called timetoevent2, which is the survival or censoring time (\(X_i\)), and a variable called event, which is the failure indicator that equals 0 for censoring and equals 1 for failure (\(\delta_i\)). To determine how many failures were observed, we can use the table command. Based on this command, there were 219 out of the 326 subjects who had a relapse.

table(relapse$event)


  0   1 
107 219 


In order to complete a survival analysis in R, we will use the survival library. To use the functions in the survival library, we will have to specify both the survival time and the failure indicator in the Surv function. When we use the Surv function, we specify the time variable first (relapse$timetoevent2) and the failure indicator second (relapse$event). In R, the failure indicator should equal 1 for subjects with the event and equal 0 for subjects who are right censored. When we try to complete analyses, R treats the Surv object as a single variable. For example, if we would like to calculate some summary statistics for this dataset we can use the survfit command with the Surv object. The results from this command are shown here:

library(survival)
survfit(Surv(relapse$timetoevent2, relapse$event)~1)

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(relapse$timetoevent2, relapse$event) ~ 
    1)

       n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
[1,] 326    219   74.7    57.2    96.2


The results from survfit show the total number of patients (326), number of who had an event (219), and the median survival time (74.658424). Note that R provides a 95% confidence interval for the median survival time as well (57.235893, 96.165894).
The more common way to write this command is to use the following form. Note the similarity between this format and the t.test command that we have used previously. In particular, the outcome is on the left of the “~” and the predictor is on the right. Since we have no predictors at this point, we include a “1” after the “~”. Finally, we specify the dataset that we are using after data.

survfit(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~1, data=relapse)

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ 1, data = relapse)

       n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
[1,] 326    219   74.7    57.2    96.2




Kaplan-Meier curve
The Kaplan-Meier curve is a nonparametric estimator of the survival distribution. One basic Kaplan-Meier curve would include the survival curve only with a label for the x-axis and y-axis. To create this Kaplan-Meier survival curve for all of the subjects in this study, we can use the plot command applied to a survfit object. Here is the default version of the Kaplan-Meier curve:

plot(survfit(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~1, data=relapse))








For this Kaplan-Meier curve, a 95% confidence interval was included on the plot too.
Now let’s look at some additional options for Kaplan-Meier curves. Please look at the plot command below. Within the survfit command, we start by declaring the two components of the time to event outcome within the Surv command as above. For this analysis, the time to event is the variable timetoevent2 and the event indicator is the variable event. The remainder of the survfit specifies that we would like to include no predictors (~1) and the dataset that we are using. All the options within the red parentheses are related to the survfit command.
In addition to the options for the survfit command, R provides us with many options that can be added to the basic Kaplan-Meier curve by adding options to the plot part of the command. In particular, all the options that are specific to the plot are included within the parentheses for the plot command. In this example, we specify that we would not like the confidence interval for the survival curve (conf.int=F), we would not like to show the censoring time points (mark.time=F), and we would like to label the x-axis and y-axis (xlab=“Weeks”, ylab=“Survival probability”). The resulting Kaplan-Meier survival curve is shown here.

plot(survfit(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~1, data=relapse), conf.int=F, mark.time=F, xlab="Weeks", ylab="Survival probability")








The Kaplan-Meier curve above shows an estimate of the survival distribution in our sample. The drops of the Kaplan-Meier curve occur at the failure times. As described in class, survival data often includes censored observations. The curve does not drop at these time points, but we can add markers for the censoring time points using the following command:

plot(survfit(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~1, data=relapse), conf.int=F, mark.time=T, xlab="Weeks", ylab="Survival probability")








Finally, we can create separate Kaplan-Meier curves for multiple groups. For this example, we will make separate Kaplan-Meier curves for the subjects based on SNP status (snp=0 for those who do not have the SNP, snp=1 for those who do have the SNP). Based on this Kaplan-Meier curve, we can see that patients in the two groups were quite similar in terms of the survival distribution.

plot(survfit(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~snp, data=relapse), conf.int=F, mark.time=F, xlab="Weeks", ylab="Survival probability", col=c("black", "red"))
legend(x="topright", legend=c("snp=0","snp=1"), col=c("black", "red"), lty=1)










Log rank test
As described in class, the log-rank test is the most commonly used approach to compare two survival distributions. Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State estimand of interest: Survival distribution in two groups (\(H_0: S_0(t)= S_1(t)\))
State type of data: Time to event outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical test: Log rank test

To test for a difference between survival curves, we can use the survdiff command. Note that this command has the same format as the survfit command for plotting the group specific Kaplan-Meier curves except we replace survfit with survdiff. In particular, we first specify survdiff. Then, we specify the survival object with the time to event and failure indicator using the Surv command and the indicator of group after ~.The following results are provided.

survdiff(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~snp, data=relapse )

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ snp, data = relapse)

        N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
snp=0 117       79     82.4    0.1363     0.219
snp=1 209      140    136.6    0.0821     0.219

 Chisq= 0.2  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.6 


The output from the log-rank test provides two main pieces of information. First, the output provides the observed number of events and the expected number of events under the null hypothesis of no group difference. We can use this part of the output to determine the direction of the association (i.e. which group had the event faster). Since the Kaplan-Meier curves were quite similar, the observed and expected values are quite similar here as well.
The second piece of information is the p-value for the hypothesis test of no difference in the survival distributions. With this information, we can complete the final three steps of our hypothesis test.

State summary statistics if possible: \(\chi^{2}=\) 0.22
Calculate p-value (stat package): \(p=\) 0.64
Based on our sample, there was a limited difference in the survival distribution between the two groups.

To fit the Gehan-Wilcoxon test, we need to add the rho=1 option to the survdiff command. In this case, there is a very small difference in the output

survdiff(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~snp, data=relapse,rho=1)

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ snp, data = relapse, 
    rho = 1)

        N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
snp=0 117     49.1     51.4    0.1049     0.235
snp=1 209     88.7     86.3    0.0625     0.235

 Chisq= 0.2  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.6

title: PCE Simple Linear Regression for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete simple linear regression in R.

Simple linear regression
Please open the bpf.csv dataset and call the dataset bpf_data. In the previous practicum, we investigated the association between age and BPF using Pearson’s correlation coefficient. We can perform the same analysis using linear regression. For this analysis, we will consider BPF as our outcome variable and age as our predictor variable. Our regression equation is given here:
\[
BPF_i=\beta_0+\beta_1*age_i+e_i
\]
As we discussed in class, \(\beta_0\) is the intercept (i.e. the mean BPF when age is equal to 0) and \(\beta_1\) is the slope (i.e. the mean change in BPF for every on unit increase in age). In this example, we are interested if there is an association between age and BPF. In terms of this regression equation, we are interested in estimating the coefficient of age \((\beta_1)\).
As always, we can complete the first three steps of our analysis before we use R:

State estimand of interest: Linear regression coefficient
State type of data: Continuous outcome, continuous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical test: Linear regression

To estimate the coefficients and associated p-values for a regression equation in R, we use the lm command, which stands for linear model. Inside the lm parentheses, we will specify the linear model that we would like to investigate. In the lm command, the outcome variable is listed on the left side of the equation, and the predictor variable is listed on the right side (bpf~age). As we will see in future practicums, we can include more than one predictor on the right side of the equation for multiple regression. Since both the predictor and outcome are in the same dataset, we use the data command to indicate the dataset we would like to use for this analysis (data=bpf_data). To display the results of the linear regression model, we can use the summary command to show the estimated coefficients and p-values. To display the confidence interval for the estimated coefficients, we can use the confint command.

mod1<-lm(bpf ~ age, data=bpf_data)
summary(mod1)


Call:
lm(formula = bpf ~ age, data = bpf_data)

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-0.071413 -0.030109 -0.003813  0.026938  0.072003 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.9574429  0.0350370  27.327  < 2e-16 ***
age         -0.0028799  0.0007845  -3.671  0.00105 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.04061 on 27 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.333, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3083 
F-statistic: 13.48 on 1 and 27 DF,  p-value: 0.001049

confint(mod1)

                   2.5 %       97.5 %
(Intercept)  0.885553035  1.029332846
age         -0.004489521 -0.001270374


The results show the estimated intercept (\(\hat{\beta}_0=\) 0.957) and the estimated slope (\(\hat{\beta}_1 =\) -0.0029, blue arrow). The estimated regression equation is shown here:
\[
\hat{BPF}=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*age
\]
The interpretation of the estimated slope is that for every one unit increase in age, the estimated mean BPF decreases by -0.0029 units. In order to test our null hypothesis that \(\beta_0=0\), R provides a p-value. The p-value is equal to 0.001. The confidence interval for the slope coefficient is -0.0045 to -0.0013. With this information, we can complete our analysis.

State estimate: \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) -0.0029
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 95% CI: -0.0045, -0.0013; \(p=\) 0.001
The estimated regression coefficient is -0.0029, and the 95% confidence interval for the linear regression coefficient for a model between age and BPF is -0.0045 to -0.0013. This confidence interval does not include the null value of 0, showing that no association between age and BPF is not one of the plausible values.

Notice that the p-value from the linear regression model and Pearson’s correlation coefficient from the previous practicum are the same. In addition, the R regression output provides an estimate of \(R^2 =\) 0.333, which also matches Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r =\) -0.577, \(r^2 =\) 0.333).

title: PCE Pairwise for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete pairwise comparisons after completing one-way ANOVA in R.

Pairwise group comparisons
Please load the diet dataset into R. We performed one-way ANOVA in the previous practicum and found that there was a difference among the groups. Here are the means in the groups as well as the p-value for the one-way ANOVA.

by(diet$weight, diet$diet, mean)

diet$diet: 1
[1] 25.4
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 2
[1] 22.3
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 3
[1] 19.9
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 4
[1] 19.8

mod1<-lm(weight~factor(diet), data=diet)
anova(mod1)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: weight
             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
factor(diet)  3  208.1  69.367  7.6367 0.0004476 ***
Residuals    36  327.0   9.083                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Since we found that at least one group is different, we would like to complete the pairwise comparisons. In order to correct for multiple comparisons, we can use a Bonferroni correction. To complete pairwise comparisons with a Bonferroni correction, we can use the pairwise.t.test command:

pairwise.t.test(diet$weight,diet$diet, p.adj = "bonf")


    Pairwise comparisons using t tests with pooled SD 

data:  diet$weight and diet$diet 

  1      2      3     
2 0.1641 -      -     
3 0.0014 0.5005 -     
4 0.0011 0.4310 1.0000

P value adjustment method: bonferroni 


The table provides the pairwise group comparisons with Bonferroni adjusted p-values. For example, the comparison of Diet 4 and Diet 1 has a p-value of 0.0011. Recall that the mean weight for Diet 1 is 25.4, while the mean weight for Diet 4 is 19.8. This pairwise comparison shows that Diet 1 leads to a higher weight.

title: PCE Paired Continuous Data for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will show how to complete the paired t-test and the Wilcoxon signed rank test in R.

Continuous outcome/paired t-test
In a recent study, we measured the intensity of brain structures on MRI on the left and right side of the brain in a group of MS patients. In this analysis, our initial question of interest will be whether there is a difference in the intensity on the left and right side of the brain. On the course website, the paired t-test dataset has been posted.
Please read in the dataset and call the dataset “mri” in R or RStudio. When we look at the dataset, we can see that the information on the left and right side of the brain is listed in separate columns. This is called wide format because the repeated measures on the patient are listed in separate columns. In this format, each row contains all information about a patient. The wide format is used for a paired t-test in R. The alternative format is the long format in which each observation has a separate row, and each patient has multiple rows.
We can calculate the mean for the two sides using the mean command that we have used previously:

mean(mri$leftside)

[1] 0.3269464

mean(mri$rightside)

[1] 0.2868738


Note that the mean is larger on the left side compared to the right side. To complete a paired t-test in R, we will use the t.test command that we have learned previously with the paired=T option. For the paired t-test, we list the two paired observations separated by a comma (blue and red arrow). We also list the paired=T option (green arrow).

t.test(mri$leftside,mri$rightside, paired=T)


    Paired t-test

data:  mri$leftside and mri$rightside
t = 2.4118, df = 9, p-value = 0.03914
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.002485629 0.077659493
sample estimates:
mean difference 
     0.04007256 


Note that the output looks very similar to the one and two-sample t-test output we have seen in previous practicums. In particular, the R output includes the estimated mean of the difference in between the left and the right side (0.04), and the 95% confidence interval for the difference between the groups (0.002, 0.078). Finally, the two-sided p-value for the hypothesis test of a difference between the sides is shown as well (0.039). Given this information, we can complete our analysis of paired data.

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Mean of difference between left and right side; \(H_0:\mu_{left}=\mu_{right}\); or \(H_0; \mu_{diff}=0\)
State type of data: Paired continuous data
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Paired t-test
State summary statistics if possible: \(\bar{x}_{diff}=\) 0.04
Calculate 95% confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 0.002, 0.078; \(p=\) 0.039
The estimated mean of the difference comparing the left side to the right side is 0.04 with a range of plausible values from 0.002 to 0.078. The left side had greater intensity.

Note that our 95% confidence interval for the difference between the left and right side also does not include 0, which agrees with the p-value from our hypothesis test being less than 0.05.


Relationship between paired t-test and one sample t-test
A paired t-test is testing whether there is a difference between the left and the right side of the brain. An alternative way to assess this question is to calculate the difference between the left and the right side of the brain. In this case, each patient would have a single difference so that we now have one observation per person and the observations are independent. To calculate this difference in R, we use:

mri$diff<-mri$leftside-mri$rightside

We would like to estimate the difference between the left side and the right side. If there was no difference between the left side and right side, the mean of the differences would be 0, and we could perform this analysis using a one-sample t-test. To complete this analysis, we use the following command and these results are provided:

t.test(mri$diff)


    One Sample t-test

data:  mri$diff
t = 2.4118, df = 9, p-value = 0.03914
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.002485629 0.077659493
sample estimates:
 mean of x 
0.04007256 


Note that the estimated difference, 95% confidence interval and p-value are exactly the same as the paired t-test. The reason for this equivalence is that the paired t-test accounts for the fact that we have two observations per patient by analyzing the difference between the measurements rather than the individual observations. Therefore, a paired t-test and a one sample t-test on the difference between the two measurements are equivalent.


Paired vs. Unpaired t-test
If we had not known that we had paired data, we might have compared the two groups using a two-sample t-test. In this case, we would be assuming that the observations on the left side are unrelated to the observations on the right side. In other words, all of the observations are independent. When the data is in wide format, we can complete a two sample t-test using a slightly different R command from the command we have learned in earlier practicums. Note that we use a comma to separate the two variables rather than the ~ we used to separate the outcome variable from the group variable previously.

t.test(mri$leftside, mri$rightside, paired=F)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  mri$leftside and mri$rightside
t = 1.2253, df = 15.812, p-value = 0.2384
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.02932549  0.10947062
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
0.3269464 0.2868738 


Note that the mean on the left side, mean on the right side, and estimated difference between these means are the same as the estimate mean of the differences, but the 95% confidence interval and p-value have changed. The reason for the change is that the paired t-test removes variability due to the patient, but the two-sample t-test does not remove this source of variability.
The choice between a paired t-test and a two-sample t-test is based on the design or how the data are collected. If you have paired data, you should incorporate this into the analysis to ensure that you reach the correct conclusion.


Wilcoxon signed rank test
Now, let’s compare these two measurements using a Wilcoxon signed rank test.
Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State null hypothesis: \(H_0:\) median difference=0,
State type of data: Continuous outcome, single sample
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Wilcoxon signed rank test

To complete this hypothesis test in R, we will use the wilcox.test command. There are two ways that we complete this test. If we have already calculated the difference, you can use the following command:

wilcox.test(mri$diff)


    Wilcoxon signed rank exact test

data:  mri$diff
V = 45, p-value = 0.08398
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0


To obtain the same result without calculating the differences, we could use this command:

wilcox.test(mri$leftside,mri$rightside, paired=T)


    Wilcoxon signed rank exact test

data:  mri$leftside and mri$rightside
V = 45, p-value = 0.08398
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


With this information, we can complete our hypothesis test.

State summary statistics if possible: Sum of positive ranks= 45
Calculate p-value (stat package): \(p=\) 0.084
Decide whether to reject or not reject the null hypothesis: Fail to reject \(H_0\).

Note that the p-value here is larger than 0.05 and the p-value from the paired t-test is smaller than 0.05. This difference shows that the conclusion regarding the difference between the groups depends on the chosen analysis. It is reasonable to report both results, but we should not choose the analysis after we look at the p-value.

title: PCE Multiple Linear Regression for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete multiple regression in R.

Multiple regression
For this practicum, we will use the bpf dataset. For this dataset, we have an outcome variable, BPF, and two continuous predictors, activity and age. Prior to fitting a multiple regression model, we should specify the hypothesis test of interest if we plan to test a hypothesis. Our primary aim is to understand if there is an association between the presence of disease activity and BPF controlling for age. Therefore, we will focus on this in our analysis.
Please load the bpf dataset into R. Activity is the indicator variable used in the example in class. The population regression equation for this analysis is
\[
BPF_i=\beta_0+\beta_1*activity_i+\beta_2*age_i+e_i
\]
In this example, we would like to assess whether there is an association between the presence of disease activity and BPF controlling for age. Although we are using a more complex model, the steps for completing our hypothesis remain the same. In this case, the coefficient of interest for this hypothesis is the coefficient of activity \((\beta_1)\). As usual, before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Difference between those with disease activity and those without disease activity holding age constant \((\beta_1)\)
State type of data: Continuous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Multiple linear regression

title: PCE Logistic regression for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to perform logistic regression in R.

Logistic regression
For this example, we will use the Logistic_regression dataset. In this dataset, we followed RRMS patients for two years. One important outcome in MS is the presence of sustained progression on the EDSS. Sustained progression is defined as a one-unit increase on the EDSS that is sustained for at least 6 months. Patients were classified as either progressed or not progressed after two years (variable name: prog). In our analysis, we would like to investigate the impact of a genetic mutation called a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP, variable name: snp) on the probability of progression. In our dataset, snp=0 for patients without the SNP, and snp=1 for patients with the SNP. We would also like to investigate the effect of age on the probability of progression.


Dichotomous predictor
As described in class, the form of the logistic regression model is similar to the linear regression model, but we focus on the log odds as the outcome. To assess the impact of the SNP on the probability of progression, we will use the following equation:
\[
log(Odds_i)=log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})=\beta_0+\beta_1*snp_i
\] The interpretation of the coefficients is:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, which means the \(log(Odds)\) when \(snp\) is equal to 0. Since \(snp=0\) is the patients without the SNP, \(\beta_0\) is the \(log(Odds)\) in patients without the SNP.
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, which is the change in \(log(Odds)\) for every on unit increase in \(snp\). In other words, \(\beta_1\) is the difference in the \(log(Odds)\) in patients with the SNP compared to those without the SNP.
In addition, the \(log(Odds)\) in patients with the SNP is \(\beta_0+\beta_1\).

We can see how the \(\beta_1\) is the difference in the \(log(Odds)\) betwen the two groups and how this is related to the \(log(OR)\) here:
\[
log(OR)=log(\frac{Odds_{SNP+}}{Odds_{SNP-}})=log(Odds_{SNP+})-log(Odds_{SNP-})=(\beta_0+\beta_1)-\beta_0=\beta_1
\]
Another interpretation of \(\beta_1\) is in terms of the odds ratio. To see the relationship, we need to remember that we can exponentiate to get rid of the \(log\).
\[
OR=\frac{Odds_{SNP+}}{Odds_{SNP-}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1}}{e^{\beta_0}}=e^{\beta_1}
\]
Therefore, \(e^{\beta_1}\) is equal to the odds ratio comparing the patients with the SNP and the patients without the SNP.
In this case, we are interested if there is an association between SNP and progression. If there was no association, \(\beta_1\) would be equal to 0, which allows us to set up our null hypothesis. As always, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test before we use R:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimand of interest: \(\beta_1\); \(H_0: \beta_1=0\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression

To estimate the parameters of the regression equation in R, we use the glm command with family set equal to binomial.

mod1<-glm(prog~ snp, data=Logistic_regression, family=binomial)
summary(mod1)


Call:
glm(formula = prog ~ snp, family = binomial, data = Logistic_regression)

Coefficients:

---

The estimated logistic regression equation is shown here:
\[
log(\hat{Odds}_i)=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i
\]
where the estimated intercept (\(\hat{\beta}_0 =\) -2.07) and the estimated slope (\(\hat{\beta}_1 =\) 0.428).
The interpretation of the estimated slope is that for every one unit increase in \(snp\), the estimated \(log(Odds)\) increases by 0.428 units. In terms of the odds ratio, the coefficient says that the odds ratio comparing patients with the SNP to those without the SNP is \(\hat{OR}=e^{\hat{\beta}_1} =\) 1.53.
In order to test our null hypothesis that \(\beta_1 = 0\), R provides both a p-value and confidence interval. The p-value is equal to 0.322, and the confidence interval for the coefficient is (-0.418, 1.273).
With this information, we can complete our analysis.

State estimate: \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) 0.428
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): -0.418, 1.273; \(p=\) 0.322
The estimated change in the log odds of progression comparing the SNP+ to SNP- is 0.428 with a range of plausible values from -0.418 to 1.273.

To calculate the estimated odds ratio, we need to calculate \(e^{\hat{\beta}_1}\) as described above. To do this, we first use the coef command to get the logistic regression coefficients.

coef(mod1)

(Intercept)         snp

To calculate the odds ratio for SNP, we need to use the exp command for the second element of coef(mod1), which is the coefficient of SNP.

exp(coef(mod1)[2])

1.533499 


To calculate the confidence interval for the odds ratio, we must use the exp command for the upper and lower limit of the confidence interval of the logistic regression coefficients. To get the confidence interval for the coefficient of SNP, we want the second row of the confint.default output from above.

confint.default(mod1)[2,]

-0.4179413  1.2730451 


To get the confidence interval for the odds ratio of SNP, we take the upper and lower limit of the regression coefficients and use exp for each.

exp(confint.default(mod1)[2,])

0.6584009 3.5717123 


Note that the null hypothesis for the odds ratio is 1. The null value is included in the interval. To complete our hypothesis test based on this output, we would complete the following steps:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimand of interest: \(OR\); \(H_0: OR=1\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression
State estimate: estimated OR = 1.53
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 0.66, 3.57; $p=$0.322
The estimated odds ratio of progression comparing the SNP+ to SNP- is 1.53 with a range of plausible values from 0.66 to 3.57.



Predicted probability
Another result from a logistic regression model is that the probability of progression can be estimated from this logistic regression model using the following relationship.
\[
log(\hat{Odds}_i)=log(\frac{\hat{p}_i}{1-\hat{p}_i})=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i
\]
\[
\hat{Odds}_1=\frac{\hat{p}_i}{1-\hat{p}_i}=e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}
\]
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}}
\]
Therefore, the predicted probability of progression in patients without the SNP is given by this formula and is equal to 0.112 using the \(\hat{\beta}_0=\) -2.07 from above.
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0}}
\]
Therefore, the predicted probability of progression in patients with the SNP is given by this formula and is equal to 0.162 using the \(\hat\beta_0=\) -2.07 and \(\hat\beta_1=\) 0.428 from above.
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1}}
\]
To calculate the predicted probability in R, we can use the predict command on the saved logistic regression model mod1 to add the predicted probability to the dataset.

Logistic_regression$predprob1<-predict(mod1, type="response")

In this command, type is the type of prediction required, where “response” gives the predicted probabilities. After typing this command, we can look at the dataset to see the predicted probabilities match what we calculated above.


Continuous predictor
For the analysis of the impact of age on the probability of progression, we will use the following equation:
\[
log(Odds_i)=log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})=\beta_0+\beta_1*age_i
\]
Note that this equation is similar to the previous example. The interpretation of the coefficients is:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, which means the log(Odds) when age is equal to 0.
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, which is the change in log(Odds) for every on unit increase in age.

To see the interpretation of \(\beta_1\) mathematically, we can use this subtraction:
\[
\begin{align}
log(OR)&=log(\frac{Odds_{age+1}}{Odds_{age}})=log(Odds_{age+1})-log(Odds_{age}) \\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1*(age+1))-(\beta_0+\beta_1*age)\\
&=\beta_1
\end{align}
\]
As in the dichotomous predictor case, another interpretation of \(\beta_1\) is in terms of the odds ratio.
\[
OR=\frac{Odds_{age+1}}{Odds_{age}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1*(age+1)}}{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1*(age)}}=e^{\beta_1}
\]
Therefore, \(e^{\beta_1}\) is equal to the odds ratio for a one unit increase in age.
In this case, we are interested if there is an association between age and progression. If there was no association, \(\beta_1\) would be equal to 0, which allows us to set up our null hypothesis. As always, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test before we use R:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimate of interest: \(\beta_1\); \(H_0: \beta_1=0\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, continuous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression

To estimate the parameters of the regression equation in R, we again use the glm command with family set equal to binomial:

mod2<-glm(prog~ age, data=Logistic_regression, family=binomial)
summary(mod2)
