title: PCE Cox for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: In this practicum, you will learn how to fit a Cox proportional hazards model in R.

Introduction
In previous classes, you have learned how linear regression extended the t-test to allow any type of predictor and multiple predictors in the same model. For a survival outcome, the Cox proportional hazards regression extends the log-rank test to allow investigation of continuous, categorical and dichotomous predictors as well as multiple predictors in the same model. Cox proportional hazards regression is the most common regression approach for analysis of a survival outcome.
For linear regression, we used the following model:
\[
E(Y_i|X_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1*x_{1i}+\beta_2*x_{2i}+\beta_3*x_{3i}
\]
In this model, we had an intercept (\(\beta_0\)) and a set of covariates with associated regression coefficients. We were able to perform analyses about the association between covariates and the outcome by focusing on \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\), or \(\beta_3\).
For Cox proportional hazards regression, we use the following model:
\[
\lambda_i(t)=\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1*x_{1i}+\beta_2*x_{2i}+\beta_3*x_{3i}}
\]
For this model, we assume that there is a baseline hazard of an event, \(\lambda_0(t)\), and the covariates multiply the hazard. Note that we do not have an intercept in this model, but the baseline hazard acts like the intercept. Similar to linear regression, we have a set of covariates with associated regression coefficients, and we are able to estimate the association between these covariates and the outcome using \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\), or \(\beta_3\).
###Single predictor
Please open the relapse.csv dataset. First, we need to load the survival library into R:

library(survival)

As we saw in previous practicums, we need to tell R the two variables involved in the time to event variable definition using the Surv option.
Here is a Kaplan-Meier curve for the time to event in each group:

plot(survfit(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~snp, data=relapse), 
col=c("black","red"))








In addition to the Kaplan-Meier curve to show the survival curves in the two groups, we can formally compare the survival distributions using the log-rank test. Here is the command and results for the log-rank test.

survdiff(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~snp, data=relapse)

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ snp, data = relapse)

        N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
snp=0 117       79     82.4    0.1363     0.219
snp=1 209      140    136.6    0.0821     0.219

 Chisq= 0.2  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.6 


Here are the steps for the hypothesis test using the log-rank test.

State estimand of interest: Survival distribution in two groups \((H_0: S_0(t)= S_1(t))\)
State type of data: Time to event outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical test: Log rank test
State summary statistics if possible: \(\chi^2=\) 0.219
Calculate p-value (stat package): \(p=\) 0.64
Based on our sample, there was a limited (no statistically significant) difference in the survival distribution between the two groups.

In addition to the log-rank test, we can compare the two groups to estimate the hazard ratio using a Cox proportional hazards model. For this analysis, we can set up our Cox proportional hazards model as
\[
\lambda_i(t)=\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1*snp_i}
\]
To demonstrate the meaning of the coefficient, we can write the hazard in each group.
No SNP: \(\lambda_{noSNP}(t)=\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1*0}=\lambda_0(t)\)
SNP: \(\lambda_{SNP}(t)=\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1*1}=\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1}\)
The hazard in the no SNP group is equal to the baseline hazard, and the hazard in the SNP group is equal to the baseline hazard multiplied by a function of the regression coefficient (\(\beta_1\)). Since the hazard in the SNP group is equal to the hazard in the no SNP group multiplied by a factor, the two hazards are proportional.
In order to calculate the hazard ratio comparing the long to the short, we get the following result:
\[
HR=\frac{\lambda_{SNP}(t)}{\lambda_{noSNP}(t)}=\frac{\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1}}{\lambda_0(t)}=e^{\beta_1}
\]
If \(\beta_1\) equals 0, the hazard ratio would equal 1. Therefore, we estimate the association between SNP status and the outcome by focusing on \(\beta_1\).
We can fit a Cox proportional hazards model using the coxph command. The coxph command is very similar to the survfit and survdiff commands that we learned in the previous practicum. In particular, we specify the Surv object with the time to event and failure indicator on the left side of the “~”. On the right side of the “~”, we list all of the predictors, just as we have with the lm command in the past. In this analysis, we only have one predictor so we only include snp on the right side of the equation. The results from the Cox model are shown here.

mod1<-coxph(Surv(timetoevent2, event)~snp, data=relapse)
summary(mod1)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ snp, data = relapse)

  n= 326, number of events= 219 

       coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z Pr(>|z|)
snp 0.06598   1.06820  0.14095 0.468     0.64

    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
snp     1.068     0.9362    0.8104     1.408

Concordance= 0.509  (se = 0.018 )
Likelihood ratio test= 0.22  on 1 df,   p=0.6
Wald test            = 0.22  on 1 df,   p=0.6
Score (logrank) test = 0.22  on 1 df,   p=0.6


Note that R provides the estimated Cox proportional hazards regression model coefficient (0.066) and exp(coef) (1.07). As we described above, exp(coef) is the hazard ratio because of the relationship between the regression coefficient and the hazard ratio shown above. In addition to the hazard ratio, R also provides the 95% confidence interval for the hazard ratio (0.81, 1.41).
Given the R output, we can complete our analysis as we have done previously.

State estimand of interest: \(HR\)
State type of data: Time to event outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical test: Cox proportional hazards model
State estimate: \(HR=\) 1.07
Calculate 95% CI and p-value: 0.81, 1.41; \(p=\) 0.64
The estimated hazard ratio comparing SNP group to no SNP group is 1.07, and the range of plausible values is from 0.81 to 1.41. A hazard ratio of 1 is included in the confidence interval.

Since the hazard ratio is greater than 1, it implies that the hazard in the SNP group is higher than the hazard in the no SNP group even though no difference between the groups is included in the confidence interval. This result matches the relationship shown in the Kaplan-Meier curve above. Note that the inference from this analysis matches the inference from the log-rank test above.
(Technical note: R actually provides three p-values at the bottom of the Cox proportional hazards model output: Likelihood ratio test, Wald test and Score (log rank) test. These p-values are testing whether the full model is better than a model with no predictors. In this case, testing whether the full model is better than a model with no predictors is the same as testing whether the coefficient for snp is equal to 0. This is why the p-value for the coefficient of snp matches the Wald p-value from the bottom of the coxph output. When we have only one predictor, the Score (log rank) test p-value will match the results from the log-rank test if we use the Breslow method to handle ties.)


Multiple predictors
The strength of the Cox proportional hazards model is the ability to include multiple predictors of the time to event outcome in a single model. This allows us to assess the independent association between multiple predictors and the outcome.
As an example, we will continue our analysis of the association between SNP status and the time to event. Now, we would like to control for disease duration our analysis. To do this, we would like to fit a model including SNP and disease duration. For this analysis, we can set up our Cox proportional hazards model as
\[
\lambda_i(t)=\lambda_0(t)*e^{\beta_1*snp_i+\beta_2*dd_i}
\] To complete our hypothesis test, we can write the first three steps before using R:

State estimand of interest: Association between SNP and the time to event holding disease duration constant (\(\beta_1\) or \(HR\))
State type of data: Time to event outcome, dichotomous predictor
Determine appropriate statistical test: Cox proportional hazards model

To fit this model in R, we use coxph and add the predictors: snp+dd. The R command and output are provided here:

mod2<-coxph(Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ snp+dd, data = relapse)
summary(mod2)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(timetoevent2, event) ~ snp + dd, data = relapse)

  n= 326, number of events= 219 

        coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
snp  0.06245   1.06444  0.14098  0.443    0.658
dd  -0.01189   0.98818  0.01109 -1.072    0.284

    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
snp    1.0644     0.9395    0.8074     1.403
dd     0.9882     1.0120    0.9669     1.010

Concordance= 0.518  (se = 0.022 )
Likelihood ratio test= 1.43  on 2 df,   p=0.5
Wald test            = 1.36  on 2 df,   p=0.5
Score (logrank) test = 1.36  on 2 df,   p=0.5


Based on these results we can complete the hypothesis test

State estimate: \(\hat{HR}=\) 1.06
Calculate 95% CI and p-value: 95% CI: 0.81, 1.4; \(p=\) 0.658
The estimated adjusted hazard ratio comparing the SNP group to no SNP group holding disease duration constant is 1.06, and the range of plausible values is from 0.81 to 1.4. A hazard ratio of 1 is included in the confidence interval.

title: PCE Correlation for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to calculate Pearson’s correlation coefficient and Spearman’s correlation coefficient in R.

Pearson’s correlation coefficient
In lecture, we investigated the association between age and BPF in a sample of MS patients. The dataset for the example is provided in the bpf.csv dataset. We would like to understand if there is an association between age and BPF in MS patients. As a first approach, we will estimate the correlation coefficient between these two measures.
Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our approach:

State estimand of interest: Correlation coefficient
State type of data: Continuous outcome, continuous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical test: Pearson’s correlation coefficient

Please read the bpf.csv dataset into R.
A reasonable first step in this analysis is to create a scatterplot of the data to ensure that we do not have any outliers or problems with data entry. To create a scatterplot in R, we use

plot(y=bpf$bpf, x=bpf$age, ylab="BPF", xlab="Age")








Based on this graph, there are no concerning outliers and there appears to be a downward trend. To calculate Pearson’s correlation coefficient, we can use the cor.test command. For this command, we list the two variables. The default method for cor.test is to calculate Pearson’s correlation coefficient so no additional options must be specified.

cor.test(bpf$bpf, bpf$age)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  bpf$bpf and bpf$age
t = -3.6713, df = 27, p-value = 0.001049
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.7788310 -0.2670003
sample estimates:
       cor 
-0.5770386 


The results show the estimated correlation coefficient (\(r=\) -0.577), along with the 95% confidence interval for the correlation coefficient (-0.779, -0.267). The p-value is for the test of whether the correlation coefficient is 0 (\(p =\) 0.001). This is a two-sided p-value. R provides the alternative hypothesis as well so that we know the p-value corresponds to a two-sided test.
With this information, we can complete our analysis. 4. State estimate: \(r =\) -0.577 5. Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 95% CI: -0.779, -0.267; \(p=\) 0.001 6. The estimated correlation between age and BPF is -0.577, and the 95% confidence interval for the correlation coefficient between age and BPF is -0.779 to -0.267. This confidence interval does not include the null value of 0, showing that no association between age and BPF is not one of the plausible values.


Spearman’s correlation coefficient
If we are interested in calculating a nonparametric correlation coefficient, the most common choice is Spearman’s correlation coefficient. Kendall’s tau is also available in R as a cor.test method (method= “kendall”), but this is less commonly used in medical statistics. The command for Spearman’s correlation coefficient is also cor.test, but we must add the method= “spearman” option.

cor.test(bpf$bpf, bpf$age, method= "spearman")


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  bpf$bpf and bpf$age
S = 6457.6, p-value = 0.0007448
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
       rho 
-0.5905396 


In this output, R provides the estimated correlation coefficient (\(r_s=\) -0.591), and the p-value for the hypothesis test regarding whether the correlation coefficient is equal to 0 (\(p=\) 0.001).

title: PCE Interaction terms for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to investigate interaction terms in linear and logistic regression using R

Multiple regression review
In class, we described how to investigate interaction terms. An interaction term implies that the effect of one predictor on the outcome is affected by another predictor in the model. Even though an interaction has a different interpretation than regression coefficients from previous models, the approach for testing for an interaction term is still based on regression coefficients.
For this practicum, we investigate the BPF dataset that we have used in previous practicums (bpf dataset). Please load this dataset into R and call the dataset bpf_data. In previous practicums, we have investigated the effect of disease activity on BPF controlling for age using the following regression equation where activity=0 for those without activity and activity=1 for those with activity:
\[
E(BPF_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1*activity_i+\beta_2*age_i
\]
In this model, there is an association between both activity \((\beta_1)\) and age \((\beta_2)\). In particular, the regression equation in those without activity is:
\[
E(BPF_i)=\beta_0+\beta_2*age_i
\]
The regression equation in those with activity is:
\[
E(BPF_i)=(\beta_0+\beta_1)+\beta_2*age_i
\] Note that in the two models, the association between age and BPF is the same in each group \((\beta_2)\), but the intercepts in the activity group and the no activity group are different. Therefore, this model assumes parallel lines with different intercepts.
To complete this regression in R, we use the following commands.

mod1<-lm(bpf ~ activity+age, data=bpf_data)
summary(mod1)


Call:
lm(formula = bpf ~ activity + age, data = bpf_data)

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-0.066041 -0.026283 -0.001167  0.028317  0.075897 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.9419854  0.0389932  24.158  < 2e-16 ***
activity     0.0171886  0.0187867   0.915  0.36864    
age         -0.0026207  0.0008363  -3.134  0.00424 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.04073 on 26 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3538,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3041 
F-statistic: 7.117 on 2 and 26 DF,  p-value: 0.003427

confint(mod1)

                   2.5 %        97.5 %
(Intercept)  0.861833605  1.0221371331
activity    -0.021428078  0.0558052356
age         -0.004339732 -0.0009016238


The resulting regression equation from this analysis is
\[
\hat{BPF}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*activity_i+\hat{\beta}_2*age_i
\]
with \(\hat{\beta}_0=\) 0.942, \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) 0.0172, and \(\hat{\beta}_2=\) -0.0026.
The corresponding graph for this regression equation can be created in R using the following commands:

bpf_data$yhat<-predict(mod1)
bpf_data<- bpf_data[order(bpf_data$age),]
plot(bpf_data$age,bpf_data$bpf,type="n",xlab="Age (years)",ylab="BPF")
points(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==1],bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==1],col="blue")
points(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==0],bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==0],col="red")
lines(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==1],bpf_data$yhat[bpf_data$activity==1],col="blue")
lines(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==0],bpf_data$yhat[bpf_data$activity==0],col="red")








Note that this regression equation assumes equal slopes for the activity group and the no activity group. In previous practicums, we have discussed how to test whether there was an association between activity and BPF controlling for age based on this model.


Interaction term
It might be important to assess whether the change in BPF with age was different in the activity group and no activity group. In other words, we might want to assess if there is an interaction between age and activity in terms of the association with BPF. The regression equation in this case is given by:
\[
E(BPF_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1*activity_i+\beta_2*age_i+\beta_3*activity_i*age_i
\] Based on this model, the regression equation for the no activity group is: \[
E(BPF_i)=\beta_0+\beta_2*age_i
\]
The regression equation for the activity group is: \[
E(BPF_i)=(\beta_0+\beta_1)+(\beta_2+\beta_3)*age_i
\] In this model, the slope and intercept were different for the two groups. Our focus for this example is to assess whether the association with age is different in the two groups. If the association with age is different, the difference in the slopes \((\beta_3)\) would be different than 0. Therefore, our focus will be this regression coefficient. As usual, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test before we run the regression in R:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Difference in slopes (i.e. interaction between age and activity; \(\beta_3\)); \(H_0: \beta_3=0\)
State type of data: Continuous outcome, dichotomous/continuous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical test: Multiple linear regression

There are a couple of ways to investigate an interaction using R. The first is to directly create the appropriate interaction term. I prefer this approach since I know exactly how the variable has been created. We would like a variable that is equal to age for the activity group and equal to 0 for the no activity group. This can be created using the following command:

bpf_data$inter<-bpf_data$age*bpf_data$activity

Since activity=0 for no activity group, the variable inter will equal 0 for no activity group because 0 times age is always equal to 0. Since activity=1 for the activity group, the variable inter will equal age for the activity group because 1 times age is always equal to age. Now, we can add this term to our lm command.

mod2<-lm(bpf ~ activity+age+inter, data=bpf_data)
summary(mod2)


Call:
lm(formula = bpf ~ activity + age + inter, data = bpf_data)

Residuals:

-0.071989 -0.026672 -0.000472  0.026953  0.075640

              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.9556349  0.0478778  19.960  < 2e-16 ***
activity    -0.0197127  0.0753469  -0.262  0.79575    
age         -0.0029210  0.0010353  -2.821  0.00924 ** 
inter        0.0009147  0.0018070   0.506  0.61714    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.04133 on 25 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3603,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2836 
F-statistic: 4.694 on 3 and 25 DF,  p-value: 0.009831

age         -0.005053254 -0.000788680
inter       -0.002806796  0.004636233


Based on this output, we get the following regression equation:
\[
\hat{BPF}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*activity_i+\hat{\beta}_2*age_i+\hat{\beta}_3*activity_i*age_i
\]
where \(\hat{\beta}_0=\) 0.956, \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) -0.0197, \(\hat{\beta}_2=\) -0.0029, and \(\hat{\beta}_3=\) 9^{-4}
Based on this model, the regression equation for the no activity group is: \[
\hat{BPF}=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_2*age_i
\]
where the intercept for the no activity group is \(\hat{\beta}_0\) 0.956, and the slope for the not activity group is \(\hat{\beta}_2=\) -0.0029.
The regression equation for the activity group is: \[
\hat{BPF}_i=(\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1)+(\hat{\beta}_2+\hat{\beta}_3)*age_i
\] where the intercept fof the activity group is \(\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1=\) 0.956 \(+\) -0.0197=0.9363, and the slope in the activity group is \(\hat{\beta}_2+\hat{\beta}_3=\) -0.0029 \(+\) 9^{-4}=-0.002
Note that the difference in the slope for the activity group and the no activity group is 9^{-4}, which is the estimated \(\hat{\beta}_3\). The graph of our predicted values from this model can be created using the following commands:

bpf_data$yhat2<-predict(mod2)
bpf_data<- bpf_data[order(bpf_data$age),]
plot(bpf_data$age,bpf_data$bpf,type="n",xlab="Age (years)",ylab="BPF")
points(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==1],bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==1],col="blue")
points(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==0],bpf_data$bpf[bpf_data$activity==0],col="red")
lines(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==1],bpf_data$yhat2[bpf_data$activity==1],col="blue")
lines(bpf_data$age[bpf_data$activity==0],bpf_data$yhat2[bpf_data$activity==0],col="red")








Based on the graph, we can see that the slopes are only a little different in the two groups. The p-value for the hypothesis test of interest is provided in the R output above (\(p=\) 0.617). Now, we can finish our analysis.

State summary statistics if possible: estimated \(\hat{\beta}_3 =\) 9^{-4}
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): -0.0028, 0.0046; \(p=\) 0.617
The estimated difference in the slopes was 9^{-4}, and the range of plausible values for the difference in the slopes is from -0.0028 to 0.0046. There is limited evidence of a statistical interaction based on our sample.

Since there was a limited difference in the slope comparing the activity group and the no activity group, we can remove this term from the model.
In addition to this approach, R allows us to investigate interactions without generating new variables, but we must be more careful in our coding. In particular, we must tell R which variables are categorical/dichotomous and which variables are continuous. For categorical/dichotomous variables, we add factor prior to the variable name. The new regression command is given here:

mod3<-lm(bpf ~ factor(activity)+age+factor(activity):age, data=bpf_data)
summary(mod3)


Call:
lm(formula = bpf ~ factor(activity) + age + factor(activity):age, 
    data = bpf_data)

Residuals:

(Intercept)            0.9556349  0.0478778  19.960  < 2e-16 ***
factor(activity)1     -0.0197127  0.0753469  -0.262  0.79575    
age                   -0.0029210  0.0010353  -2.821  0.00924 ** 
factor(activity)1:age  0.0009147  0.0018070   0.506  0.61714    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.04133 on 25 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3603,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2836 
F-statistic: 4.694 on 3 and 25 DF,  p-value: 0.009831

(Intercept)            0.857028615  1.054241130

age                   -0.005053254 -0.000788680
factor(activity)1:age -0.002806796  0.004636233


The factor(activity):age part of the command indicates to R that we would like to investigate the interaction between these two variables. Note that the results from this command are exactly the same as from the previous analysis. The factor(activity)1 in the regression output indicates that the coefficient is for patients with activity=1. This demonstrates that R is using no activity group as the reference group. Also, the factor(activity)1:age indicates that the coefficient is the difference in the slopes comparing the disease activity group to the no disease activity group. This coding can be helpful if you have a categorical variable with many levels.


Interaction terms in logistic regression
Let’s return to the Logistic_regression dataset. In the logistic regression lab, we investigated a couple of univariate relationships between variables and the probability of progression in MS patients. In addition to these analyses, we might be interested in whether the effect of one variable changes in the presence of a second variable. As we learned with linear regression, we can fit interaction terms to investigate this specific hypothesis. In this case, we would like to know if the association between SNP and progression is different in disease activity group and no disease activity group. Here is the logistic regression model that we would like to fit
\[
log(Odds_i)=log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})=\beta_0+\beta_1*SNP_i+\beta_2*activity+\beta_3*SNP_i*activity_i
\]
To investigate this hypothesis, we must create the interaction term and then fit the following model.

Logistic_regression$inter<- Logistic_regression$activity* Logistic_regression$snp
mod4<-glm(prog~ snp+ activity+ inter, data=Logistic_regression, family=binomial)
summary(mod4)


Call:
glm(formula = prog ~ snp + activity + inter, family = binomial, 
    data = Logistic_regression)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) -2.07944    0.33540  -6.200 5.65e-10 ***
snp          0.38485    0.49398   0.779    0.436    
activity     0.04256    0.69950   0.061    0.951    
inter        0.18570    1.01542   0.183    0.855    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 147.96  on 189  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 146.89  on 186  degrees of freedom
AIC: 154.89

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

(Intercept) -2.7368176 -1.422065

Based on these results, we can complete our hypothesis test:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Difference in association between SNP and progression in the disease activity group compared to the no disease activity group (\(\beta_3\)); \(H_0: \beta_3=0\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical test: Logistic regression
State summary statistics if possible: \(\hat{\beta}_3=\) 0.186
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): (-1.804, 2.176); \(p=\) 0.855
The estimated difference in the association is 0.186, and the range of plausible values is from -1.804 to 2.176. No difference in association between SNP and progression in the activity group and no activity group is included in the plausible values.



Relationship to Mantel-Haentzel tests
When we want to control for the potential confounding effect of activity, we could use a Mantel-Haentzel approach. This approach creates a 2x2 table for each group and then combines across the tables. To perform this analysis in R, we use the following command:
The output from this analysis shows many things. First, the crude and Mantel-Haenszel adjusted RR (green arrow) and OR (blue arrow) are reported. In the middle, there is a “Test for homogeneity” for both the RR and OR. This test is asking whether the effect of SNP on progression is the same in the two groups. Note that there is limited evidence that the effect of SNP is different in the two groups for the RR (p=0.861, orange arrow) and the OR (p=0.861, red arrow). Please note that this is the same p-value and conclusion that we arrived at when we tested for an interaction between activity and SNP in our logistic regression model (orange arrow above). The Mantel-Haenszel test and logistic regression provide two alternative ways to think about the same hypothesis.

title: PCE Oneway ANOVA for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete one-way ANOVA in R.

One-way ANOVA
Please load the diet dataset into R.
For this example, we were interested in the impact of four different diets (Diet 1, Diet 2, Diet 3, Diet 4) on the weight (in grams) of mice. In all, 40 mice (10 per group) contributed to our experiment. Our null hypothesis is that the mean in each of the groups will be the same (\(\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\)), and our alternative hypothesis is that at least one of the groups is different. Since we have a continuous outcome with a categorical predictor, we will analyze this data using one-way ANOVA.
Since one-way ANOVA will start with an assessment of whether the four groups have the same mean, we will start with the steps for a hypothesis test:

State null hypothesis in terms of association of interest
State type of data
Determine appropriate statistical approach
State estimate of association
Calculate p-value and confidence interval
Decide whether to reject or not reject the null hypothesis

Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State null hypothesis in terms of association of interest: \(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\), \(H_A:\) at least one mean is different
State type of data: Continuous outcome, categorical predictor
Determine appropriate statistical approach: ANOVA

Now, we will summarize and graph the data to ensure that we do not have any outliers or data entry issues. To do this, we will use the by and boxplot commands.
The following command summarizes the variable weight in each diet group separately. To learn more about the by command, please type ?by. In this help file, you will note that the first part of the command is the data that we would like to investigate, the second part of the command defines the groups, and the third part of the command lists the function that we would like to use in each of the groups.

by(diet$weight, diet$diet, summary)

boxplot(diet$weight~diet$diet, xlab="Diet", ylab="Weight")








Since there are no obvious outliers or other issues with the data, we will proceed to complete our analysis. The first approach to do this is to use the aov and summary functions. The aov function fits a one-way ANOVA model, and we use the summary function to see the output. In a this analysis, we can use:

mod1<-aov(diet$weight~factor(diet$diet))
summary(mod1)

Note that we must specify here factor(diet$diet) so that R knows that the variable diet is a categorical variable rather than a continuous variable. If we did not specify factor, R would treat diet as a continuous variable.
This command tests the null hypothesis from above (\(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\)).
The p-value is 4^{-4}, which is less than 0.05. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that at least one of the means is different. To formally complete our hypothesis test, we complete the remaining steps.

mod2<-lm(weight~factor(diet), data=diet)

We could also have analyzed this dataset using the Kruskal-Wallis test. The Kruskal-Wallis test would be the more appropriate analysis if we believed that the normality assumption did not hold for our dataset. To complete the Kruskal-Wallis test in R, we use the kruskal.test command shown here:

title: PCE Paired Dichotomous Data for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will show how to complete McNemar’s test and kappa statistics in R.

McNemar’s test
Please open the McNemar_test.csv dataset from the course website and call it mcnem. This dataset provides the data described in the lecture. In particular, the dataset includes the relapse status at year 1 and year 5 for each of the 178 subjects. This dataset is in wide format because the repeated measures on the patient are listed in separate columns. In this format, each row contains all information about a patient. The wide format is required for a McNemar’s test in R.
The alternative format is the long format in which each observation has a separate row, and each patient has multiple rows. The long format will be required to use the Mantel-Haenszel approach for paired data. There is a link between McNemar’s test and the Mantel-Haenszel approach that you will learn about in future courses.
In order to see the number and proportion of subjects who had a relapse at each year, we can use the tabulate command that we have learned in previous practicums.

table(mcnem$year1)


  0   1 
133  45 

prop.table(table(mcnem$year1))


       0        1 
0.747191 0.252809 

table(mcnem$year5)


  0   1 
142  36 

prop.table(table(mcnem$year5))


        0         1 
0.7977528 0.2022472 


As we can see, 45 subjects had a relapse in year 1, which corresponds to 0.253 of the subjects. A smaller proportion of subjects had a relapse in year 5. In particular, only 36 subjects had a relapse in year 5, which corresponds to 0.202. To see the discordant and concordant pairs, we can use the table command.

table(mcnem$year1, mcnem$year5)

   
      0   1
  0 123  10
  1  19  26


On this table, the presence/absence of a relapse at year 1 is the row variable, and the presence/absence of a relapse at year 5 is the column variable. Therefore, the number of subjects who had a relapse at year 5 and no relapse at year 1 is 10, and the number of subjects who had a relapse at year 1 and no relapse at year 5 is 19.
Despite the difference in the proportion, we would like to formally compare the groups. Since we observed the same subjects at the two time points, we must account for the pairing in the analysis using McNemar’s test. One approach for fitting McNemar’s test in R is to use the mcnemar.test command and output are shown here.

mcnemar.test(mcnem$year1, mcnem$year5)


    McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction

data:  mcnem$year1 and mcnem$year5
McNemar's chi-squared = 2.2069, df = 1, p-value = 0.1374


Note that the output looks similar to the output from the chisq.test command that we have seen in previous practicums. As with the chisq.test command, the default is to include a continuity correction. The resulting p-value is slightly different than the p-value the lecture and Stata because of the continuity correction, but the conclusion is similar.
If we would like to match the results from the lecture and Stata, we can add correct=F to the command.

mcnemar.test(mcnem$year1,mcnem$year5,correct=F)


    McNemar's Chi-squared test

data:  mcnem$year1 and mcnem$year5
McNemar's chi-squared = 2.7931, df = 1, p-value = 0.09467


In order to calculate the exact p-value for McNemar’s test and the confidence interval for the odds ratio, we can use the mcnemar.exact command from the exact2x2 library. In R, there are many additional commands that we can use for specialized analyses that require loading additional libraries. You need to install the exact2x2 first (install.packages(exact2x2)), and then we can load this library.

library(exact2x2)

Loading required package: exactci


Loading required package: ssanv


Loading required package: testthat


Now, we can use the mcnemar.exact command in a similar way to how we used the mcnemar.test command, but we get different statistics:

mcnemar.exact(mcnem$year1,mcnem$year5)


    Exact McNemar test (with central confidence intervals)

data:  mcnem$year1 and mcnem$year5
b = 10, c = 19, p-value = 0.136
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2185962 1.1896487
sample estimates:
odds ratio

The two-sided p-value for the exact McNemar’s test of a difference between the years is shown 0.136. In addition, the estimated odds ratio (0.53) and 95% confidence interval for the odds ratio (0.22, 1.19) are provided.
Given this information, we can complete our McNemar’s test.

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimand of interest: Association between year and presence of relapse; \(H_0: OR=1\)
State type of data: Paired dichotomous data
Determine appropriate statistical test: McNemar’s test
State summary statistics if possible: \(\hat{OR}=\) 0.53

The estimated OR comparing year 5 to year 1 is 0.53 with a range of plausible values from 0.22 to 1.19. Note that an OR of 1 indicating no difference between the years is included in the confidence interval, but the interval is quite wide given our limited sample size.

title: PCE Practicum Power for R
text:
Program in Clinical Effectiveness
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete sample size and power calculations for one and two sample t-tests in R.

One sample t-test
A common scenario in medical research is when a new set of patients is compared to a historical control group with known mean. As an example, assume that we know the mean score on a math test using traditional teaching techniques is 85 with a standard deviation of 20. We have a new program that we believe will improve performance and lead to a mean score of 95. We can recruit 50 students and would like to know the power we will have to detect our hypothesized difference.
In this scenario, we are collecting a single sample and we will compare the observed data to a hypothesized mean value using a one sample t-test. Remember for a study of this type, there are five pieces of information of interest:

Type I error rate (alpha level)
Difference between the means of the null and alternative hypotheses
Standard deviation of the data
Sample size
Power

We need to know four of these five pieces of information to calculate the final piece. The type I error rate is almost always chosen to be 0.05 based on a two-sided test. The standard deviation is 20 based on the information above, and we will assume that the standard deviation in our new group is the same as in the historical data. The null hypothesis in this example is that the mean on the new program is equal to 85 (\(H_0: \mu_0=85\)), and the alternative hypothesis is that the mean is equal to 95 (\(H_A: \mu_A=95\)). The sample size is 50.
Given this information, we can calculate the power to detect the proposed difference using the power.t.test command in R.
For this command, we enter the difference between the groups (delta=(95-85)), the standard deviation (sd=20), the sample size (n=50), type I error rate (sig.level=0.05), the type of t-test (type=“one.sample”), and the direction of the alternative hypothesis (alternative=“two.sided”).

power.t.test(delta=(95-85), sd=20, n=50, sig.level=0.05,type="one.sample", alternative="two.sided")


     One-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 50
          delta = 10
             sd = 20
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9338976
    alternative = two.sided


The results show that the power for the proposed study is 93.4.
As a follow-up, we might be interested in the sample size required to have 80% power. For this, we can also use the power.t.test command, but we must specify the power rather than the sample size (power=0.8)

power.t.test(delta=(95-85), sd=20, power=0.8, sig.level=0.05,type="one.sample", alternative="two.sided")


     One-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 33.3672
          delta = 10
             sd = 20
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided


Since we always round up, R shows that the sample size required for 80% power is 34.
Note that the command to calculate the power or the sample size is the same. R will calculate either the power or sample size depending on what is not included in the power.t.test command.


Two sample t-test
The more common scenario in medical research is a comparison of two groups. An alternative approach to investigate the question from the previous study would be to compare one group of students taught with the traditional teaching technique and another group of students taught with the new technique. Let’s assume that the mean in the traditional teaching group is 85, the mean in the new technique group is 95 and the standard deviation in each group is 20.
In this scenario, we are collecting two samples and we will compare the mean in the two samples using a two sample t-test. Remember for a study of this type, there are five pieces of information of interest:

Type I error rate (alpha level)
Difference between the means of the null and alternative hypotheses
Standard deviation in each group (we assume it is equal for this function)
Sample size
Power

We need to know four of these five pieces of information to calculate the final piece. The type I error rate is chosen to be 0.05 based on a two-sided test. The standard deviation is 20 in each group based on the information above, and it is reasonable to assume they are equal based on the information above. The mean in the traditional program is 85 and the postulated mean under the new program is 95. Therefore, the null hypothesis in this example is that the mean in each program is equal to 85 \((H_0: \mu_1-\mu_2=0)\), and the alternative hypothesis is that the mean in the new program is 10 units higher \((H_A: \mu_1-\mu_2=10)\). The desired power for this study is 80%.
Given this information, we can calculate the sample size required for 80% power to detect the proposed difference using the power.t.test command in R.
For this command, we enter the difference between the groups (delta=(95-85)), the standard deviation (sd=20), power (power=0.8), type I error rate (sig.level=0.05), type of t-test (type=“two.sample”), and the direction of the alternative hypothesis (alternative=“two.sided”).

power.t.test(delta=(95-85), sd=20, power=0.8, sig.level=0.05,type="two.sample", alternative="two.sided")


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 63.76576
          delta = 10
             sd = 20
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


Since we should always round up, the results show that we will need 64 patients per group to detect the proposed difference. This corresponds to a total sample size for the study of 128.


Two sample test of proportions
We would like to the effect of a treatment on the recurrence of disease in mice. We will consider recurrence of disease as a dichotomous variable. The proportion of mice that will have a recurrence in the placebo group is 0.7. We hypothesize that the proportion of mice that will have a recurrence in the treated group is 0.4. How many mice per group will we need to have 80% power to detect the proposed difference using a two sample test of proportions/chi-square test?
To calculate the power for a comparison of two proportions, we need to use the power.prop.test command in R. For this command, we enter the proportions in the two groups (p1=0.4, p2=0.7), power (power=0.8), and type I error rate (sig.level=0.05). Note that we do not need to specify a standard deviation in this case because the standard deviation of a proportion is related to the proportion.

power.prop.test(p1=0.4, p2=0.7, sig.level=0.05, power=0.8)


     Two-sample comparison of proportions power calculation 

              n = 41.97025
             p1 = 0.4
             p2 = 0.7
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group

title: PCE Oneway ANOVA for R
text:
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete one-way ANOVA in R.


Please load the diet dataset into R.
For this example, we were interested in the impact of four different diets (Diet 1, Diet 2, Diet 3, Diet 4) on the weight (in grams) of mice. In all, 40 mice (10 per group) contributed to our experiment. Our null hypothesis is that the mean in each of the groups will be the same (\(\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\)), and our alternative hypothesis is that at least one of the groups is different. Since we have a continuous outcome with a categorical predictor, we will analyze this data using one-way ANOVA.
Since one-way ANOVA will start with an assessment of whether the four groups have the same mean, we will start with the steps for a hypothesis test:

State null hypothesis in terms of association of interest
State type of data
Determine appropriate statistical approach
State estimate of association
Calculate p-value and confidence interval
Decide whether to reject or not reject the null hypothesis

Before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State null hypothesis in terms of association of interest: \(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\), \(H_A:\) at least one mean is different
State type of data: Continuous outcome, categorical predictor
Determine appropriate statistical approach: ANOVA

Now, we will summarize and graph the data to ensure that we do not have any outliers or data entry issues. To do this, we will use the by and boxplot commands.
The following command summarizes the variable weight in each diet group separately. To learn more about the by command, please type ?by. In this help file, you will note that the first part of the command is the data that we would like to investigate, the second part of the command defines the groups, and the third part of the command lists the function that we would like to use in each of the groups.

by(diet$weight, diet$diet, summary)

diet$diet: 1
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  20.00   24.25   25.50   25.40   27.75   29.00 
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 2
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  17.00   19.50   23.00   22.30   24.75   28.00 
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 3
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  16.00   17.25   20.00   19.90   21.75   25.00 
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 4
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  16.00   18.00   20.00   19.80   20.75   24.00 


If we would like to calculate the standard deviation in each group, we could use the same by command, but we would change the function to sd.

by(diet$weight, diet$diet, sd)

diet$diet: 1
[1] 2.836273
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 2
[1] 3.529243
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 3
[1] 2.923088
------------------------------------------------------------ 
diet$diet: 4
[1] 2.699794


We can also create group specific box plots:

boxplot(diet$weight~diet$diet, xlab="Diet", ylab="Weight")








Since there are no obvious outliers or other issues with the data, we will proceed to complete our analysis. The first approach to do this is to use the aov and summary functions. The aov function fits a one-way ANOVA model, and we use the summary function to see the output. In a this analysis, we can use:

mod1<-aov(diet$weight~factor(diet$diet))
summary(mod1)  

                  Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
factor(diet$diet)  3  208.1   69.37   7.637 0.000448 ***
Residuals         36  327.0    9.08                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Note that we must specify here factor(diet$diet) so that R knows that the variable diet is a categorical variable rather than a continuous variable. If we did not specify factor, R would treat diet as a continuous variable.
This command tests the null hypothesis from above (\(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\)).
The p-value is 4^{-4}, which is less than 0.05. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that at least one of the means is different. To formally complete our hypothesis test, we complete the remaining steps.

State summary statistics: \(\bar{x_1}=\) 25.4 grams, \(\bar{x_2}=\) 22.3 grams,\(\bar{x_3}=\) 19.9 grams, \(\bar{x_4}=\) 19.8 grams
Calculate p-value (stat package): \(p=\) 4^{-4}
Decide whether to reject or not reject the null hypothesis: Reject \(H_0\)

An alternative approach to perform a one-way ANOVA is to use the anova function combined with the lm function. The anova function extracts the ANOVA table from the linear model fitted by the lm function.

mod2<-lm(weight~factor(diet), data=diet)
anova(mod2)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: weight
             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
factor(diet)  3  208.1  69.367  7.6367 0.0004476 ***
Residuals    36  327.0   9.083                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


As expected, the p-value for the main hypothesis is the same as using aov.



We could also have analyzed this dataset using the Kruskal-Wallis test. The Kruskal-Wallis test would be the more appropriate analysis if we believed that the normality assumption did not hold for our dataset. To complete the Kruskal-Wallis test in R, we use the kruskal.test command shown here:

kruskal.test(weight~factor(diet), data=diet)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  weight by factor(diet)
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 14.885, df = 3, p-value = 0.001918


Note that the p-value (0.0019) is not the same as the one-way ANOVA p-value, but it is similar and the inference would be the same in this case.

title: PCE Practicum Summary Statistics for R
text:
Goal: This practicum will go over how to calculate summary statistics and how to make simple graphics in R.


In lecture, we investigated summary statistics and basic graphics. In this practicum, we will learn how to calculate summary statistics and create graphics in R.
Please read the digitalis_dataset_23.csv dataset into R by following the steps from the previous document and call the dataset dig for the remaining code below. R is case sensitive. This means that you should check if the variable names are uppercase or lowercase. In the remainder of this practicum, we will use lowercase for the variable names, but you can adjust as needed.
On Canvas, we also provide a PDF describing the Digitalis trial, which was a multicenter trial with more than 300 centers in the US and Canada. This trial aimed to estimate the efficacy and safety of Digoxin in treating patients with congestive heart failure. A teaching version of the dataset has been made available by the NHBLI, and information related to the dataset is also provided on Canvas. Please note that this dataset is only a subset of the full dataset available from NHBLI.
An important first step in many studies is to calculate summary statistics related to baseline characteristics in the sample. To calculate the summary statistics for a continuous variable, the R command summary can be used. Let’s investigate baseline age using the summary. For this command, we write the command first (summary). Then, inside the parentheses we list the dataset name before the dollar sign (dig) and the variable name within the dataset after the dollar sign (age). The following output is produced:

summary(dig$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.62   71.00   90.00 


In this output, R provides the minimum (21), median (65), mean (63.6), and maximum (90).
We can also calculate additional summary statistics using separate commands. Note that for these commands, we would need to add the na.rm=T option if there were missing observations in the dataset. Here are the commands and output for calculating the mean, standard deviation, and variance.

mean(dig$age)

[1] 63.61786

sd(dig$age)

[1] 10.85402

var(dig$age)

[1] 117.8098


If we would like to calculate the median, minimum and maximum, we can use the following commands:

median(dig$age)

[1] 65

min(dig$age)

[1] 21

max(dig$age)

[1] 90


If we would like to calculate other percentiles, we can use the quantile command with the probs option to indicate the percentile we are interested in. As an example, this command will calculate the 25th and 75th percentiles.

quantile(dig$age, probs=c(0.25, 0.75))

25% 75% 
 57  71 


To calculate the skewness and kurtosis, we need to install a separate library. In R, there are libraries that we can install with additional commands.

library(e1071)
skewness(dig$age)

[1] -0.5246339

kurtosis(dig$age)

[1] 0.2909112





R has the ability to create many graphics. Although there are advanced R packages to create plots, we will focus on basic R commands at this early stage. When we make plots in RStudio, the resulting plots are shown in the lower right-hand window. We can copy and paste the plots or save the plots using the Export button above the plot.
For the histogram of age, we use the following command.

hist(dig$age, xlab="Age", main="Histogram of Age")








For this command, age is the variable name for the variable of interest. The other two options tell R the title of the x-axis and the title of the graph.
For the box plot of age, we use the following command:

boxplot(dig$age, ylab="Age", main="Box plot of Age")











In the dataset, the variable “sex” is a dichotomous variable, so the summary statistic of interest is the proportion of males and females. As described above, sex=1 for male and sex=2 for the female. To calculate the frequency and proportion of males and females in the dataset, we can use the table and prop.table commands.

table(dig$sex)


   1    2 
4216 1227 


This command provides the number of males (4216) and females (1227).

prop.table(table(dig$sex))


        1         2 
0.7745728 0.2254272 


This command provides the percent of males (0.7745728) and females (0.2254272).



In addition to the summary statistics in the entire sample, we would often like to calculate the summary statistics in each sex separately. In R, there are a number of ways to calculate the group specific summary statistics. One approach to calculate the age in each group is to subset the data and calculate the summary statistics in each subset. To subset the data, we can choose the rows from the dataset with sex=1. Then, we can calculate the summary statistics of the age in this subset.
For this command, note that we have the same information as the original summary command from above. In particular, we are applying the summary command (summary) to the variable age from the dataset dig. The main change is that we have added [dig$sex==1,] . When we use the [], we are trying to look at a subset of the data. When we have a data frame, there are both rows and columns. The rows that we would like to focus on are identified before the comma, and the columns after the comma. By writing dig$sex==1 before the comma, we indicate that we would like the rows in which sex is equal to 1. Since we have nothing after the comma, we indicate that we would like all the columns. The result is that dig[dig$sex==1,] finds the rows in the dig dataset in which sex is equal to 1, and then the rest of the command find the summary statistics for the variable age. We can use the same concept for sex equal to 2.

summary(dig[dig$sex==1,]$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  22.00   57.00   65.00   63.54   71.00   90.00 

summary(dig[dig$sex==2,]$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.89   71.00   90.00 


An alternative approach is to use the by command. In this command, we state the variable we are interested in (dig$age), the variable that identifies the groups (dig$sex), and the function we would like to apply to the variable (summary).

by(dig$age, dig$sex, summary)

Goal: This practicum will go over how to calculate summary statistics and how to make simple graphics in R.


In lecture, we investigated summary statistics and basic graphics. In this practicum, we will learn how to calculate summary statistics and create graphics in R.
Please read the digitalis_dataset_23.csv dataset into R by following the steps from the previous document and call the dataset dig for the remaining code below. R is case sensitive. This means that you should check if the variable names are uppercase or lowercase. In the remainder of this practicum, we will use lowercase for the variable names, but you can adjust as needed.
On Canvas, we also provide a PDF describing the Digitalis trial, which was a multicenter trial with more than 300 centers in the US and Canada. This trial aimed to estimate the efficacy and safety of Digoxin in treating patients with congestive heart failure. A teaching version of the dataset has been made available by the NHBLI, and information related to the dataset is also provided on Canvas. Please note that this dataset is only a subset of the full dataset available from NHBLI.
An important first step in many studies is to calculate summary statistics related to baseline characteristics in the sample. To calculate the summary statistics for a continuous variable, the R command summary can be used. Let’s investigate baseline age using the summary. For this command, we write the command first (summary). Then, inside the parentheses we list the dataset name before the dollar sign (dig) and the variable name within the dataset after the dollar sign (age). The following output is produced:

summary(dig$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.62   71.00   90.00 


In this output, R provides the minimum (21), median (65), mean (63.6), and maximum (90).
We can also calculate additional summary statistics using separate commands. Note that for these commands, we would need to add the na.rm=T option if there were missing observations in the dataset. Here are the commands and output for calculating the mean, standard deviation, and variance.

mean(dig$age)

[1] 63.61786

sd(dig$age)

[1] 10.85402

var(dig$age)

[1] 117.8098


If we would like to calculate the median, minimum and maximum, we can use the following commands:

median(dig$age)

[1] 65

min(dig$age)

[1] 21

max(dig$age)

[1] 90


If we would like to calculate other percentiles, we can use the quantile command with the probs option to indicate the percentile we are interested in. As an example, this command will calculate the 25th and 75th percentiles.

quantile(dig$age, probs=c(0.25, 0.75))

25% 75% 
 57  71 


To calculate the skewness and kurtosis, we need to install a separate library. In R, there are libraries that we can install with additional commands.

library(e1071)
skewness(dig$age)

[1] -0.5246339

kurtosis(dig$age)

[1] 0.2909112





R has the ability to create many graphics. Although there are advanced R packages to create plots, we will focus on basic R commands at this early stage. When we make plots in RStudio, the resulting plots are shown in the lower right-hand window. We can copy and paste the plots or save the plots using the Export button above the plot.
For the histogram of age, we use the following command.

hist(dig$age, xlab="Age", main="Histogram of Age")








For this command, age is the variable name for the variable of interest. The other two options tell R the title of the x-axis and the title of the graph.
For the box plot of age, we use the following command:

boxplot(dig$age, ylab="Age", main="Box plot of Age")











In the dataset, the variable “sex” is a dichotomous variable, so the summary statistic of interest is the proportion of males and females. As described above, sex=1 for male and sex=2 for the female. To calculate the frequency and proportion of males and females in the dataset, we can use the table and prop.table commands.

table(dig$sex)


   1    2 
4216 1227 


This command provides the number of males (4216) and females (1227).

prop.table(table(dig$sex))


        1         2 
0.7745728 0.2254272 


This command provides the percent of males (0.7745728) and females (0.2254272).



In addition to the summary statistics in the entire sample, we would often like to calculate the summary statistics in each sex separately. In R, there are a number of ways to calculate the group specific summary statistics. One approach to calculate the age in each group is to subset the data and calculate the summary statistics in each subset. To subset the data, we can choose the rows from the dataset with sex=1. Then, we can calculate the summary statistics of the age in this subset.
For this command, note that we have the same information as the original summary command from above. In particular, we are applying the summary command (summary) to the variable age from the dataset dig. The main change is that we have added [dig$sex==1,] . When we use the [], we are trying to look at a subset of the data. When we have a data frame, there are both rows and columns. The rows that we would like to focus on are identified before the comma, and the columns after the comma. By writing dig$sex==1 before the comma, we indicate that we would like the rows in which sex is equal to 1. Since we have nothing after the comma, we indicate that we would like all the columns. The result is that dig[dig$sex==1,] finds the rows in the dig dataset in which sex is equal to 1, and then the rest of the command find the summary statistics for the variable age. We can use the same concept for sex equal to 2.

summary(dig[dig$sex==1,]$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  22.00   57.00   65.00   63.54   71.00   90.00 

summary(dig[dig$sex==2,]$age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.89   71.00   90.00 


An alternative approach is to use the by command. In this command, we state the variable we are interested in (dig$age), the variable that identifies the groups (dig$sex), and the function we would like to apply to the variable (summary).

by(dig$age, dig$sex, summary)

dig$sex: 1
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  22.00   57.00   65.00   63.54   71.00   90.00 
------------------------------------------------------------ 
dig$sex: 2
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   57.00   65.00   63.89   71.00   90.00

title: PCE Practicum MH for R

Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete a stratified analysis and complete a Mantel-Haenszel test in R.


Please load the MHanalysis.dta dataset into R. We are going to investigate the relationship between the presence or absence of a SNP and the presence or absence of disease progression as we did in the previous practicum for 2x2 tables. In this practicum, we will extend the ideas to stratify on a third variable and perform the Mantel-Haenszel approach.
As a first step in most analyses, we perform a crude analysis, which estimates the association between the predictor (SNP+ vs. SNP-) and the outcome (Prog+ vs. Prog-) without accounting for other variables. This is the same as the 2x2 table analysis from the previous practicum. There are several commands that we can use for this in R, but we will use the riskratio and oddsratio commands from the epitools library since it provides multiple summary statistics in a single command:

library(epitools)
riskratio(x=MHanalysis$snp,y=MHanalysis$prog)

This output shows the crude RR, which is the estimated RR from the previous analysis that did not account for age category (1.45). Note that this matches the RR from the previous crude analyses. The M-H combined RR is the RR combining over the three groups (1.46). Note that there is only a small difference between the crude and adjusted RR in this case that they appear to be the same, but this does not have to be the case in general. The 95% confidence interval for each of the RRs are also provided. The 95% CI for the adjusted RR includes 1 (0.7, 3.04).
The final part of the output provides a test for homogeneity, which is asking whether the RR in the age categories are equal. The p-value is large (\(p=\) 0.47), showing that there is no evidence that there is a difference in the RR in the three groups.
Note that the crude OR (1.53), adjusted OR (1.56) and test for homogeneity of the ORs (0.54) are all presented in the output as well.

title: PCE Logistic regression for R
text:
Goal: This practicum will go over how to perform logistic regression in R.


For this example, we will use the Logistic_regression dataset. In this dataset, we followed RRMS patients for two years. One important outcome in MS is the presence of sustained progression on the EDSS. Sustained progression is defined as a one-unit increase on the EDSS that is sustained for at least 6 months. Patients were classified as either progressed or not progressed after two years (variable name: prog). In our analysis, we would like to investigate the impact of a genetic mutation called a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP, variable name: snp) on the probability of progression. In our dataset, snp=0 for patients without the SNP, and snp=1 for patients with the SNP. We would also like to investigate the effect of age on the probability of progression.



As described in class, the form of the logistic regression model is similar to the linear regression model, but we focus on the log odds as the outcome. To assess the impact of the SNP on the probability of progression, we will use the following equation:
\[
log(Odds_i)=log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})=\beta_0+\beta_1*snp_i
\] The interpretation of the coefficients is:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, which means the \(log(Odds)\) when \(snp\) is equal to 0. Since \(snp=0\) is the patients without the SNP, \(\beta_0\) is the \(log(Odds)\) in patients without the SNP.
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, which is the change in \(log(Odds)\) for every on unit increase in \(snp\). In other words, \(\beta_1\) is the difference in the \(log(Odds)\) in patients with the SNP compared to those without the SNP.
In addition, the \(log(Odds)\) in patients with the SNP is \(\beta_0+\beta_1\).

We can see how the \(\beta_1\) is the difference in the \(log(Odds)\) betwen the two groups and how this is related to the \(log(OR)\) here:
\[
log(OR)=log(\frac{Odds_{SNP+}}{Odds_{SNP-}})=log(Odds_{SNP+})-log(Odds_{SNP-})=(\beta_0+\beta_1)-\beta_0=\beta_1
\]
Another interpretation of \(\beta_1\) is in terms of the odds ratio. To see the relationship, we need to remember that we can exponentiate to get rid of the \(log\).
\[
OR=\frac{Odds_{SNP+}}{Odds_{SNP-}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1}}{e^{\beta_0}}=e^{\beta_1}
\]
Therefore, \(e^{\beta_1}\) is equal to the odds ratio comparing the patients with the SNP and the patients without the SNP.
In this case, we are interested if there is an association between SNP and progression. If there was no association, \(\beta_1\) would be equal to 0, which allows us to set up our null hypothesis. As always, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test before we use R:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimand of interest: \(\beta_1\); \(H_0: \beta_1=0\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression

To estimate the parameters of the regression equation in R, we use the glm command with family set equal to binomial.

mod1<-glm(prog~ snp, data=Logistic_regression, family=binomial)
summary(mod1)


Call:
glm(formula = prog ~ snp, family = binomial, data = Logistic_regression)

The estimated logistic regression equation is shown here:
\[
log(\hat{Odds}_i)=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i
\]
where the estimated intercept (\(\hat{\beta}_0 =\) -2.07) and the estimated slope (\(\hat{\beta}_1 =\) 0.428).
The interpretation of the estimated slope is that for every one unit increase in \(snp\), the estimated \(log(Odds)\) increases by 0.428 units. In terms of the odds ratio, the coefficient says that the odds ratio comparing patients with the SNP to those without the SNP is \(\hat{OR}=e^{\hat{\beta}_1} =\) 1.53.
In order to test our null hypothesis that \(\beta_1 = 0\), R provides both a p-value and confidence interval. The p-value is equal to 0.322, and the confidence interval for the coefficient is (-0.418, 1.273).
With this information, we can complete our analysis.

Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): -0.418, 1.273; \(p=\) 0.322
The estimated change in the log odds of progression comparing the SNP+ to SNP- is 0.428 with a range of plausible values from -0.418 to 1.273.

To calculate the estimated odds ratio, we need to calculate \(e^{\hat{\beta}_1}\) as described above. To do this, we first use the coef command to get the logistic regression coefficients.

coef(mod1)

To calculate the odds ratio for SNP, we need to use the exp command for the second element of coef(mod1), which is the coefficient of SNP.

To calculate the confidence interval for the odds ratio, we must use the exp command for the upper and lower limit of the confidence interval of the logistic regression coefficients. To get the confidence interval for the coefficient of SNP, we want the second row of the confint.default output from above.

To get the confidence interval for the odds ratio of SNP, we take the upper and lower limit of the regression coefficients and use exp for each.

0.6584009 3.5717123 


Note that the null hypothesis for the odds ratio is 1. The null value is included in the interval. To complete our hypothesis test based on this output, we would complete the following steps:

State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression
State estimate: estimated OR = 1.53
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 0.66, 3.57; $p=$0.322
The estimated odds ratio of progression comparing the SNP+ to SNP- is 1.53 with a range of plausible values from 0.66 to 3.57.




Another result from a logistic regression model is that the probability of progression can be estimated from this logistic regression model using the following relationship.
\[
log(\hat{Odds}_i)=log(\frac{\hat{p}_i}{1-\hat{p}_i})=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i
\]
\[
\hat{Odds}_1=\frac{\hat{p}_i}{1-\hat{p}_i}=e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}
\]
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}}
\]
Therefore, the predicted probability of progression in patients without the SNP is given by this formula and is equal to 0.112 using the \(\hat{\beta}_0=\) -2.07 from above.
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0}}
\]
Therefore, the predicted probability of progression in patients with the SNP is given by this formula and is equal to 0.162 using the \(\hat\beta_0=\) -2.07 and \(\hat\beta_1=\) 0.428 from above.
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1}}
\]
To calculate the predicted probability in R, we can use the predict command on the saved logistic regression model mod1 to add the predicted probability to the dataset.

Logistic_regression$predprob1<-predict(mod1, type="response")

In this command, type is the type of prediction required, where “response” gives the predicted probabilities. After typing this command, we can look at the dataset to see the predicted probabilities match what we calculated above.



For the analysis of the impact of age on the probability of progression, we will use the following equation:
\[
log(Odds_i)=log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})=\beta_0+\beta_1*age_i
\]
Note that this equation is similar to the previous example. The interpretation of the coefficients is:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, which means the log(Odds) when age is equal to 0.
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, which is the change in log(Odds) for every on unit increase in age.

To see the interpretation of \(\beta_1\) mathematically, we can use this subtraction:
\[
\begin{align}
log(OR)&=log(\frac{Odds_{age+1}}{Odds_{age}})=log(Odds_{age+1})-log(Odds_{age}) \\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1*(age+1))-(\beta_0+\beta_1*age)\\
&=\beta_1
\end{align}
\]
As in the dichotomous predictor case, another interpretation of \(\beta_1\) is in terms of the odds ratio.
\[
OR=\frac{Odds_{age+1}}{Odds_{age}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1*(age+1)}}{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1*(age)}}=e^{\beta_1}
\]
Therefore, \(e^{\beta_1}\) is equal to the odds ratio for a one unit increase in age.
In this case, we are interested if there is an association between age and progression. If there was no association, \(\beta_1\) would be equal to 0, which allows us to set up our null hypothesis. As always, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test before we use R:

State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, continuous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression

To estimate the parameters of the regression equation in R, we again use the glm command with family set equal to binomial:

mod2<-glm(prog~ age, data=Logistic_regression, family=binomial)
summary(mod2)

In order to test our null hypothesis that \(\beta_1 = 0\), R provides both a p-value and confidence interval. The p-value is equal to 0.322, and the confidence interval for the coefficient is (-0.418, 1.273).
With this information, we can complete our analysis.

State estimate: \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) 0.428
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): -0.418, 1.273; \(p=\) 0.322
The estimated change in the log odds of progression comparing the SNP+ to SNP- is 0.428 with a range of plausible values from -0.418 to 1.273.

To calculate the estimated odds ratio, we need to calculate \(e^{\hat{\beta}_1}\) as described above. To do this, we first use the coef command to get the logistic regression coefficients.

coef(mod1)

(Intercept)         snp

To calculate the odds ratio for SNP, we need to use the exp command for the second element of coef(mod1), which is the coefficient of SNP.

exp(coef(mod1)[2])

1.533499 


To calculate the confidence interval for the odds ratio, we must use the exp command for the upper and lower limit of the confidence interval of the logistic regression coefficients. To get the confidence interval for the coefficient of SNP, we want the second row of the confint.default output from above.

confint.default(mod1)[2,]

-0.4179413  1.2730451 


To get the confidence interval for the odds ratio of SNP, we take the upper and lower limit of the regression coefficients and use exp for each.

exp(confint.default(mod1)[2,])

    2.5 %    97.5 % 
0.6584009 3.5717123 


Note that the null hypothesis for the odds ratio is 1. The null value is included in the interval. To complete our hypothesis test based on this output, we would complete the following steps:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimand of interest: \(OR\); \(H_0: OR=1\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression
State estimate: estimated OR = 1.53
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): 0.66, 3.57; $p=$0.322
The estimated odds ratio of progression comparing the SNP+ to SNP- is 1.53 with a range of plausible values from 0.66 to 3.57.




Another result from a logistic regression model is that the probability of progression can be estimated from this logistic regression model using the following relationship.
\[
log(\hat{Odds}_i)=log(\frac{\hat{p}_i}{1-\hat{p}_i})=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i
\]
\[
\hat{Odds}_1=\frac{\hat{p}_i}{1-\hat{p}_i}=e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}
\]
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*snp_i}}
\]
Therefore, the predicted probability of progression in patients without the SNP is given by this formula and is equal to 0.112 using the \(\hat{\beta}_0=\) -2.07 from above.
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0}}
\]
Therefore, the predicted probability of progression in patients with the SNP is given by this formula and is equal to 0.162 using the \(\hat\beta_0=\) -2.07 and \(\hat\beta_1=\) 0.428 from above.
\[
\hat{p}_i=\frac{e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1}}{1+e^{\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1}}
\]
To calculate the predicted probability in R, we can use the predict command on the saved logistic regression model mod1 to add the predicted probability to the dataset.

Logistic_regression$predprob1<-predict(mod1, type="response")

In this command, type is the type of prediction required, where “response” gives the predicted probabilities. After typing this command, we can look at the dataset to see the predicted probabilities match what we calculated above.



For the analysis of the impact of age on the probability of progression, we will use the following equation:
\[
log(Odds_i)=log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i})=\beta_0+\beta_1*age_i
\]
Note that this equation is similar to the previous example. The interpretation of the coefficients is:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, which means the log(Odds) when age is equal to 0.
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, which is the change in log(Odds) for every on unit increase in age.

To see the interpretation of \(\beta_1\) mathematically, we can use this subtraction:
\[
\begin{align}
log(OR)&=log(\frac{Odds_{age+1}}{Odds_{age}})=log(Odds_{age+1})-log(Odds_{age}) \\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1*(age+1))-(\beta_0+\beta_1*age)\\
&=\beta_1
\end{align}
\]
As in the dichotomous predictor case, another interpretation of \(\beta_1\) is in terms of the odds ratio.
\[
OR=\frac{Odds_{age+1}}{Odds_{age}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1*(age+1)}}{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1*(age)}}=e^{\beta_1}
\]
Therefore, \(e^{\beta_1}\) is equal to the odds ratio for a one unit increase in age.
In this case, we are interested if there is an association between age and progression. If there was no association, \(\beta_1\) would be equal to 0, which allows us to set up our null hypothesis. As always, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test before we use R:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Estimate of interest: \(\beta_1\); \(H_0: \beta_1=0\)
State type of data: Dichotomous outcome, continuous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Logistic regression

To estimate the parameters of the regression equation in R, we again use the glm command with family set equal to binomial:

mod2<-glm(prog~ age, data=Logistic_regression, family=binomial)
summary(mod2)

title: PCE Multiple Linear Regression for R
text:
Goal: This practicum will go over how to complete multiple regression in R.


For this practicum, we will use the bpf dataset. For this dataset, we have an outcome variable, BPF, and two continuous predictors, activity and age. Prior to fitting a multiple regression model, we should specify the hypothesis test of interest if we plan to test a hypothesis. Our primary aim is to understand if there is an association between the presence of disease activity and BPF controlling for age. Therefore, we will focus on this in our analysis.
Please load the bpf dataset into R. Activity is the indicator variable used in the example in class. The population regression equation for this analysis is
\[
BPF_i=\beta_0+\beta_1*activity_i+\beta_2*age_i+e_i
\]
In this example, we would like to assess whether there is an association between the presence of disease activity and BPF controlling for age. Although we are using a more complex model, the steps for completing our hypothesis remain the same. In this case, the coefficient of interest for this hypothesis is the coefficient of activity \((\beta_1)\). As usual, before we look at the data, we can complete the first three steps of our hypothesis test:

State estimand of interest and null hypothesis: Difference between those with disease activity and those without disease activity holding age constant \((\beta_1)\)
State type of data: Continuous outcome, dichotomous explanatory variable
Determine appropriate statistical approach: Multiple linear regression

To complete the appropriate multiple regression model, we will use the same command that we have previously used, lm, but we will have two predictors after the outcome variable.

mod2<-lm(bpf ~ activity+age, data=bpf_data)
summary(mod2)


Call:
lm(formula = bpf ~ activity + age, data = bpf_data)

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-0.066041 -0.026283 -0.001167  0.028317  0.075897 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.9419854  0.0389932  24.158  < 2e-16 ***
activity     0.0171886  0.0187867   0.915  0.36864    
age         -0.0026207  0.0008363  -3.134  0.00424 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.04073 on 26 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3538,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3041 
F-statistic: 7.117 on 2 and 26 DF,  p-value: 0.003427

confint(mod2)

                   2.5 %        97.5 %
(Intercept)  0.861833605  1.0221371331
activity    -0.021428078  0.0558052356
age         -0.004339732 -0.0009016238


The resulting regression equation from this analysis is
\[
\hat{BPF}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1*activity_i+\hat{\beta}_2*age_i
\]
with \(\hat{\beta}_0=\) 0.942, \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) 0.0172, and \(\hat{\beta}_2=\) -0.0026.
We discussed in class the interpretation of each of the coefficients. In particular:

The estimated mean BPF in the no disease activity group at age 0 is 0.942. Remember that activity=0 for the no activity group.
The estimated difference in BPF between the disease activity group and the no disease activity group holding age constant (or controlling for age) is 0.0172.
The estimated change in BPF for a one unit increase in age holding activity constant (or controlling for activity) is -0.0026.

To complete our analysis, we can use the R output to calculate the 95% confidence interval and p-value.

State estimate: \(\hat{\beta}_1 =\) 0.0172
Calculate confidence interval and p-value (stat package): -0.0214, 0.0558; \(p=\) 0.369
The estimated difference in mean BPF comparing the disease activity group and the no disease activity group holding age constant is 0.0172, and the range of plausible values is -0.0214 to 0.0558.

Therefore, based on our analysis, the confidence interval for the association between activity and BPF controlling for age includes no association.
